div.p: S MARRIAGE A FAILURE?

What a question to ask, but how often could it be answered' in the affirmative, the prinApal cause being the Improvidence. of Furnishing on the Hire System. Since our advertisements have appeared pointing out the disadvantages we have re- ceived several he ters agreeing with our denunciations of this pernicious sys em. Each Hire Agreement specifies that after the deposit is paid, so many weekly payments shall be made and that until the whole of the sum mentioned is paid the goods shall not become the property of the would-be pur- chaser. and that if any of the payments are neglected to the exact time specified the goods may be forcibly taken away and the whole of the payments forfeited. County Court judges have denounced the sy-tern, inasmuch as the vendor gets both money and goods. Again, the pries charged are enormous, without any respect being paid to the quality, its many cases being worn out before they are paid for. To com- bat this system, and open the eyes ot the public, Worsley's of "The Pantheon," Gaythorn. Manchester. the Largest Retailers of Second-hand Furniture in the worl4, have determined to allow all respectable householders to have furniture at the ticketed marked cash price, a small percentage being charged for the conven ence of payment by the week, month, or quarter. On the fourth page of the "Examiner" we Avertise a list of Bargains every week, any of which can be had and paid for by convenient intervals, the articles being delivered upon the first payment being made. Furniture from £5 to £1 000 may be arninged for in this way. To give an idea of the equity of our proposals we are prepared to supply for a working man a House of Furniture complete, thoroughly good and substantial (every article warranted), price £2O cash down, not a penny less, or 10 per cent extraif credit is given, maging £22. Full particulars sent on application.

The Queen has ordered several Irish poplins for the trousseau of Princess /ills of Hesse. , Messrs. Atkinson. of College Green, Dublin, are supplying, the dress lengths, all of which are of a very beauti- ful description. 17•,-..e are in white and gold, the latter being itdi metal woven in fi.i.e threads, Sometimes torming tile pattern, and at others simply outlining the satin brocade. On one of these dresses, the design is of the Louis XV. period, small curves and festoons of white satin being displayed upon the poplin ground, the who% scattered over with =ail gold shamrocks. The gold threads, where they pass at the back from one shamrock to another, give a very rich effect to the pure whiteness of the Silk, making it look as though shot with gold. Another of the white poplins is in a crescent pat- tern of an Oriental description, the crescents bein,,-; in relief in satin, and every one of them outlined in gold.

The Battersea district of London may be taken as it Constituency representing on the whole as advanced democratic ideas as are to be found grouped together in the metropolis. In watching the growth of its democratic programme, therefore, one gets as good a notion as is to be found of the trend of working-class opinion, and of what capital rtay expect in the nearer stages of the political development of the working classes. Now, in that constituency an agitation has just begun upon a great scale for an extraordinary service of extremely Cheap workmen's trains in all directions for the convenience of the workmen of that locality. The prograinme even includes the building of a new fitation, lower fares by the steamboats, and earlier and cheaper accommodation by- the tramcars. Great local demonstrations are to be held in sup- tort of these demands, and 41eput a tions all routicl will be immediately at work calling upon directors and managers, and so on. This is worth taking note of, for it is the greatest development of the kind that has yet taken place in London, and it is an indie.ation of what eapital has to expect when the V7orking democracy are able to dictate the policy of the country.

This has been the worst season known for many years with regard to the propagation of cage birds. Eggs have been hatched, but the variations of tem- perature have incemntly proved fatal to the chicks. Thus the show of the London aLd Provincial Orni- thological Society, field on Tuesday at the Royal Aquarium, was a comparative failure. In fact, there was only one mule—a charming little bird, however, crossed beween a canary and a goldfinch. The curious capped Norwich canaries which seem to have a sort of brown waterfall on the tops of their heads were noticeable, though not perhaps al- together aclmirable. Next year if there are more favourable conditilns of temperature the Society Ouglit to assert itself in much better form.

The cactus was the main feature on Tuesday at the Royal Horticultural Society's Show. It is not a pretty plant, though it used often—one hardly knows why—to be seen in cottage windows in the /Corti). Amateurs do not care to cultivate it be- tause it requires a special house to itself and can- not be grown in the general greenhouse. More- over, the cactus has to be treated varioudy. Many kinds come from the hottest and most arid regions 43f the world, but one species riloices to be buried in snow. Most of our leading florictilturists con- tributed to this day's show,and medals forcactuses were awarded to Mr. G. Pritchard and Messrs. Can- cel' and Sons. The former showed a remarkably line specimen of Germs trianplatis, which high up on its stem throws out aerial roots to catch hold ot rocks and banks and suck mOisture from them.

The persistent refusal of the Chancellor of the Exchequer to make any statement in regard to the Course of business until after the Budget is disposed of has given rise to a great deal of fresh specula- tion. The.question is even being once more freely put whether the Government may not contemplate in certain unfavourable citcurn-tances dissolving Allis year after all. ,The Attercliffe election is said tobave proved that the Budget is fully understood and highly popular with the working classes. It Is declared, indeed, by people who ()tight to be in a position to form a judgment in the matter that Mr. Langley owed the unexpectedly large unijority • which be obtained in spite of the split in the pari y to this feeling more than to any ling else. Meat.- While, it seems to become clearer day by day that the Government can hardly hope to do much effec- tive business this sesaion at ter the Budget is done with. And, it is said, it is , doubtful if next year the' can pass the measures of first-rate importance as, for instance.. Welsh Disestablishment and "One man one vote"—which may be left over. Would it not, therefore. some •of the Liberals are (taking, be otter all a good stroke of policy to -go to the country without delay? I do not yen Lure to may how much substance there may be in this new development of speculation—probably enough it Las no better basis than the score of other rumours which have cropped up during this remarkable Eession,—but it is certain that the idea that we may after all have a general election this year is not confined to the gossigs of the rank and tile. 1 know that in certain ex-official Unionist quarters the belief is very strongly entertained that if the 4aorernment have not decided to dissolve they are at least keeping this course open to themselves as a possible solution of existing difficulties.

A family gathering of a most interesting and almost unique character took place on Monday afternoon at Montague House, Whitehall, the town residence of the Duke of Buccleuch,on the occasion of the eigLty-second birthday of the Dowager rachess of Abercorn. In order to celebrate that event, all tier Grace's children, grandchildren, ard .gr,nit grandchildren—in all one hundred and one I),!rsotie, ranging in age from sixty years to tour ..onths—assembled to cile.r their congratulations to ti-se venerable lady. Many of them had travelled for the purpose from distant parts of the kingdom, and some even from America.

Th, r. is an interesting sequel to the 'establish- ment of Mr. Chamberlain's new London Municipal 13ociety. The purpose of this organisation is to win the capital to what has been described as " muni- cipal Unionism." Somehow,. however, the first tffect of the " semi-progressive line which the 'society has .adupted has been to disappoint the Vory landlords. Notwithstanding the adherence of the Duke of Norfolk, they have in certain casrs re- fused to associate themselves with the new move- 'pt. saying that the programme is a bad imitation •Of Radicalism.

I understand that the attitude of the 'Welsh Inde- readent, mrtnbers towards the Government remains exactly what it was. The announcement of the Govenrment programme may he made the- occasion •cf a renewed protest in the interest of Welsh dis- •establishment, and it is underst-od that. they will decline to support the Government on any question ' -other than the Registration Bill.

The Parliamentary Committee of the NationaV Ejotm Union met on Uednesday, with Mr. Phiiip ftanhope in the chair, and decided to take measured to obtain from the Government some decisive state- Iment of policy in regaid to the question of the, 'Luse ot Lords veto. They will.see what can he dcne this session, and if they fail they will return to the charge early next session. Probably their first effort in this direction will take the form of tillestions to be put in the House of Ccmmons. The Cotatnittte also desires to urge the Government. to give facilities this session for passing the Mines Bill through all its stages. A COLUMUtilerttiOU on the point will be sent to the Cnancellor of the Exche- ,-cuer.

div.head: LADIES' LETTER.
div.p: LADIES' LETTER.

MT DEAREST NELLIE, I have seen specimens of some open coat costumes, and a costume suitable for ohildren. The open coat costumes are almost identical in style but of dif• ferent material, the one made in cheviot serge, the other in twill drill, which are in either a pretty holland colour or drab, awl the model is of that capital shade which used to be associated with nankeen, namely, a yellow holland tinge, like a duck's foot. Toe skirt is well cut and wide, with a cross-cut back; and would prove a boon to any young ladies who are desirous of a country or seaside costume. The jacket has revers like the 1,,,pe1s of a man's coat. The child's suit has a triple row of narrow braid on the top of the skirt, and the bodice is made full, with a pointed serge • belt, and large full sleeves—a comfortable school snit, and quite in unison with the fashions. Boat- ing and tennis gowns are indispensable, and on fine days, a loose cool blouse should take the place of the regular bodice.

A modern boat shaped hat is edged with ostrich 'tips, the crown surrounded with chartreuse satin ribbon, veiled in spangled tulle. lhe bonnets for elderly ladies combine comfort with elegance, and the new veils in black net are embroidered in cream. A fine chip is interwoven with gold thread, and trimmed with spangled lace and a bunch of black violets on the crown, two jetted Mercures giving it a becoming width. A "ripe corn" fancy straw is also trimmed with bunches of black violets, and accordion-pleated tulle to match the colour of the s:-raw. A black and gold straw has a scarf of tulle wound round it and drawn through a jet buckle, a j- t star with osprey on the crown, and a bunch of cherries on the brim. A gold guipure has a bird of paradise aigrette' with two bunches of black and white violets. These bonnets are worn either with or without strings, according to taste. A dainf,y little capote of fancy pink and green straw is tzuhr,,cd with upstanding loops and ends of green and ph_ k satin riiibon, and two green mercury wings powdered with jet. Another of tabac straw ha l a wreath of ivy and buds ani two blackbirds, rising from a nest of black jetted pompons' and saudel mauve roses. Charming is a hat of black and cinnamon crinoline, with jetted net pompons, and some beautiful damask rises nestling under the brim and at toe back. A cream Leghorn hat, designed :or a bridesmaid, is

trimmed with white ostrich feathers and knot. of orange velvet and white moire. A pretty bonnet of waved jetted net is lightened with a bow of pink ribbon and two small jetted plumes and ospreys; in the front is a jet medallion. A close-fitting bonnet is covered almost entirely with pink geraniums, veiled with some cream-coloured gut- pure. Two 'black wings and a large bow across the crown formed the garniture. A delightful hat Is of green s: raw draped with black and white tulle, caught with ears of jet, and on either aide of the front an osprey stands sentinel. The new style of children's dress consists of a tight-fitting bodice out square back and front, reaching to the waist, on to which the full skirt is gathered, while the guirnpe, which is invariably of white muslin, tucked and striped with insertion, is made with full sleeves gathered into tight cuffs. The bodices are trimmed in various ways, some- times bearing braces of black watered ribbon to tie on the shoulders, at other times giving evidence of the industry of the mothers, with hand embroidery in the front, the embroidery again appearing on the hem of the full skirt. A charming frock which I know, made in this style, is of turquoise-blue cloth, with a large pattern embroidered in black

A late issue of the Melbourne " Argus " contains this advertisement : "Persons contemplating marriage may have ceremony solemnised anywhere, one pound, by fully accredited minister. Appointments now arranged, day or night, by H. Hanslow, jeweller, 307, Elizabeth- at. Needy people free." Good advice on marriage is given by the Bishop of Liverpool. He save, "Young men ought to beware of carelessness of choice in marriage. Many a young man has begun well in every way, and then by marrying a Jezebel has spoiled the whole course of his life." He ; warns them not to be in a hurry. " MArry in haste and repent at leisure " is a very old. saying, and a true one. Fora bridegroom to be jilted at the altar on the we-I- , aing morning and in full view of air the wedding guests Must be about as trying an experience as any which falls to the lot of man. Very few there be who have the nerve to face it az a Melbourne bridegroom some rears ago. He simply strolled around Collins-at., collected a couple of dozen of his friends, and adjourned to the Vienna Ca fe, where much fizz was uncorked in honour of his lucky escape.
Kitchen Cloths.

An easy way of washing kitchen dal's, and of avoid- ing the unpleasant smell arising therefrom,is the follow- ing. Soap the cloths, put them loosely ia a jar, pour over cold water, to which has been added a spoonful of liquid ammonia, to cover them, and set the jar the last thin,: at night in a cool oven which has been used for cooking. In the morning the cloths will be as nearly as possible clean, and will • need only to be rinsed, wrong out and dried.

The eyes are nearly always weak in children recovering from measles diphtheria, scarlet fever, and whooping cough ; hence children after these diseases should not be hurried off to school. THE DOUBLE LIFE;
OR, THE HAMPTON MYSTERY.
By the Author of " DARKWOOD,"
CHAPTER XXL

A GLIMMER OF THE TRITTII. Thou art come to answer A stony adversary, an inhuman wretch Incapable of pity, void and empty From every drachm of mercy. SHAKESPEARE. The disguised Lady Beatrice started as Lord Adlowe entered his uncle's parlour, and instinct- ively put up .her hand to lower her veil as he halt- ed momentarily between her and the door. The act immediately excited his lordship's at- tention, and he bestowed upon -her a keen and curious glance. He obtained, in the dim half-light, a glimpse only of a painfully white face, with cheeks on which a seemingly hectic flush burned hotly, a pair of gold-bowed spectacles, a mass of yellow hair combed low on a slightly wrinkled forehead, and two long yellow curls, and then the thick veil dropped, and her ladyship moved towards the threshold. Adlowe's gaze followed her. As her ungloved hand, so small so daintily white, with slender, tapering fingers, and pink, almond-shaped nails— contrasting so strongly with the assumed rotund- ity of her figure and pretended age—rested upon the door-knob, his lordship gave a slight start, and bent forward with a half repressed eagerness. The next moment the Lady Beatrice turned, bowed, and disappeared, closing the door behind her. With an apparent COM.:,iotBECE.S. that he had been guilty of rudeness, Lord Aeliown greeted Giralda and his uncle with profuse politeness, and then quietly sauntered, to a window and looked down into the street. "Who is that lady, uncle?" he enouired, care- lessly, fixing his eyes upon a waiting cab below. "A recent acquaintance of yours, I suppose. I don't remember ever seeing her before." , "She is the mother of my adopted (laughter, Adlowe," remarked the marquis, coldly—" the . Countess of Arevalo." Lord Adlowe uttered an ejaculation of surprise, and a strange expression, as of bellied cunning, gleamed for a moment in his pale eyes as he in- voluntaiily retreated several steps from the win- dow. "That lady her mother t" he muttered, in tones of keen disappointment, half aloud. " Impossi- ble ! Why, I thought—l fancied—" He checked himself abruptly, and returned to the window. His downward glance caught a glimpse of feminine drapery disappearing within the open door of the cab, and the next moment he beheld the vehicle depart at a rapid pace down the street. "The Countess of Arevalo!" he exclaimed, flinging himself into the chair her ladyship had recently occupied, and looking from the marquis to Giralda, who had quietly turned on the gas- light and retreated to a distant corner. "The title is not familiar to me. Is her ladyship an En- glish woman ?" "She is an Englishwoman, married to a Span- iard of rank," replied Lord Trevelyan, adjusting his gouty foot. "Her ladyship is an actress or prima donna." "Indeed !" exclaimed Adlowe significantly, as it seemed to the tortured, spirited Giralda a "I have not heard the name before." " Her ladyship has a stage name, of course," said the marquis. "She would not have her title in everybody's mouth. That accounts for your never having heard of her, although an equally good reason might be found in your eight years' absence in the East." "True," declared Adlowe, somewhat reluctant- ly, as if he were being convinced against his will. " Her ladyship," he added, " is a woman of strik- ing appearance. She had the majestic form suited to a Medea. I fancied, however, that her hand, which strikingly resembles one I have seen- some- where lately in its perfect shape, colour and- deli- cacy, was too small to accord well with her per- son." He directed a glance of gloomy suspicion at Gir- aids as he spoke, but the maiden's face was turned away, and he could not mark its expression. He observed, however, that her slight figure betrayed no mental disturbance. . If she was undisturbed, not so the marquis. He moved uneasily in his chair, thereby torturing himself, and exclaimed testily : "By the Lord Harry ! things have come to a fine pass in these degenerate °clays, when every jackanape can criticise the size of a lady's hand, and its proportion to her person. These are you: foreign manners, air. I suppose they are Oriental ; but I want no More of them sir. Du you hear I want no more of them. Be kind enough to re- member, my lord," and the tone of the marquis became intensely cutting, "that Miss Arevalo is my especial charge, being my adopted daughter, • and that any remark concerning her or her rela- tives I shall regard as personal—as personal, sir !" Lord Trevelyan sank back in his chair as he con- cluded, scowling upon his nephew, and groaning with physical pain. Adlowe hastened to make the required apolo- gies, protesting that his remark had sprung from thoughtlessness. "Humph !" ejaculated the marquis. "Thought- lessness at your age ! A giddy, thoughtless boy of forty ! Humph !" and he sneered. "Just touch that bell, Adlowe," he added. "I want that wretched Wigby to help me into an easy po- sition. I am in agony." Lord Adlowe performed the required service, and the sleek valet made his appearance. Gir- alda noticed, at his entrance, that a subdued and stealthy glance of recognition and meaning passed between the noble visitor and the valet, and she immediately sprang to the conclusion that there existed between the couple a secret acquain- tance. She stored away the fact for future use. "I am going home to-morrow," observed the marquis, when he had been made comfortable, and Wigby had withdrawn. " Giralda prefers the old Park to this foggy, gloomy London. I wish I had been well enough to escort her to Hyde Park and about town, but the gay town sights must be defer- red until a future visit." "You will scarcely be well enough to travel to- morrow, uncle," suggested Lori Adlowe. "I shall be quite well enough," asserted the marquis, with a grim smile. "My foot is grow- ing better continually under these cooling lotions ; and besides well or ill I shall go. There is no- thing like determination to carry one through a disagreeable affair." " If 1 might venture to advise you, uncle," said Lord Adlowe, "I should suggest that you re- main in town a month, put yourself under the treatment of some famous physician, and intro- duce Miss Arevalo into society. I am sure she would create a sensation. You could readily find her a suitable chaperon. Your favourite the Lady Beatrice Hampton, would no doubt gladly intro- duce your protds&" He looked at Giralda keenly, and the marquis's gaze was also turned inquiringly upon the mai- den. What do you say, my dear ? " inquired the old lord, with a fatherly smile which thoroughly transfigured his gruff face. "Do you want to stay? Speak freely, my child. It will give me pleasure to grant any wish that you may form." " I do not wish to stay' my lord," replied Gir- oda., looking up, bravely, but speaking in a voice that quivered in spite of her efforts to preserve its steadiness. "I love the Park, and I do hope you will be able to go back to-morrow." "There !" exclaimed the marquis, triumphantly, tureing upon his nephew, " what do you think of that dec6lotl, sir? You see tnat all women are not fond of gayety and frivolous society. You see," he added, in an undertone, with au exultant smile," that old and gruff and cross as I am —a miser, and all that—my society is yet desired and I am really loved by a beautiful and lovely young girl." Lord Adlowe became thoughtful. "It is a pity," he said, after a brief pause, "that Miss Arcvalo should not at least taste the cup of pleasure. She will not carry from London a shade pleasant remembrance, unless it be of her vi-it to • the theatre. By the way," be added, fixing a glance upon Gicalda's face, " It was sitigul:w that the Lady Beatrice Hampton mlnnild ha NU tainted dead away, at sight of Aliss evalo. I had always , supposed, as the world did. that her ladyship will as emotionless as a statue. What could have caused her to feint ?" " Might it not diave been the heat ?" asked the young girl, raising i•er wondrous blue eyes, now , dark and liquid aud glowing, to Adlowe's face, with a wonderful self-ootinnaud. "I felt ill lay- self about the same time." Her coolness and utter lack of emotion almost staggered Adlowe's conviction of a secret between , the Lady Beatrice Hampton and his uncle's young prot6f.r.ee. On beholding her strange emotion e-t the theatre, he had conceived, as the reader

knows, a host of suspicions, orwhich hail been I rudely shocked by the day's experiences. The visit with which his lordship had threatened the Lady Beatrice after her return home from the theatre, on the previous evening had been made during the afternoon preceding his visit to his uncle, but her ladyship's manner, in response to his inquiries, had been at once so cool and defiant and haughty, that he had begun to believe him- self utterly mistaken. The glimpse he had had of the Countess of Arevalo on his entrance into his uncle's parlour, had further mystified him ; and lastly, Giralda had given a rude shock to the ideas he had conceived. "I am either the most foolishly suspicious of men," he thought, looking at the bright, dark face , of the maiden, "or the keenest and shrewdest ! The Lady Beatrice and this young girl have either been grossly wronged by me in my thoughts, or there is some strange and deep mystery between them which even I cannot solve. I shall not re- main long in my present uncertainty." At this juncture Giralda arose, excused herself, and quietly withdrew, departing to her own chamber, desirous of sparing herself further cross-examination Pet the hands of her .parents' enemy, "A beautiful girl!" said Lord Adlowe, when the door had closed behind her. "A perfect boon! Do you really intend to adopt her as your daugh- ter, my lord?" "I intend to keep her with me as long as she will stay," returned the marquis, stiffly. " I shall make provision for her future to-morrow. My lawyer will visit me in the morning, bringing with him my will for signature." "Miss Arevalo is a fortunate young lady," observed Adlowe, lightly. "No doubt you will leave her a pretty penny, my lord.' " shall settle upon her over sixty thousand pounds." said the marquis, quietly. A greedy look came over Adlowe's face. It was he who had spread the report of his uncle's miserly character—it was he who had instilled into his cousin Geoffery the belief that Lord Trevelyan was a miser—while avarice and love of money had been the besetting sins of his own nature. The announcement of his lordship's intentions gave him a terrible pang. "Sixty thousand pounds to go to a stranger !" he exclaimed bitterly. " Uncle, you are being imposed upon by a clever adventuress!" "Sir r thundered the old marquis, with a look before which the villainous nephew shrank. "Be- ware how you speak of one whom I love, and whose good name is my especial charge! I warn you, beware !" "But, uncle," said Adlowe, deprecatingly, you pretend to be just. Is this just to rob me of what I have always expected ?" "You had no right to expect my savings. The income is mine absolutely, to use as I please." "But I need money, my lord. lam seriously embarrassed in my affairs," said Adlowe, earnee,ly. "My own estates came to me encumbered with mortgages. I have always looked forward to com- ing into the Trevelyan property as a slave looks forward to freedom. My debtors have been induced to wait until that happy period—you see I speak freely. I have counted upon yotn savings to- clear my own heavily mortgaged property. It is madness to think of leaving this money to a young girl of whose existence you did not dream a month ago ! " "Of that I must be permitted to judge for my- self," exclaimed Lord Trevelyan, haughtily. "The world will say that you are in your dotage." "What do I care for the world?" cried the mar- quis, with a magnificent scorn. "Your friends will laugh at you ! " " Then they will prove themselves not my friends, and I will not give up a cherished plan to please my enemies." "Think of my debts and necessities, uncle—"

The old marquis sneered. "Think of my years of loneliness," he returned, "'when you never came near me. Think of the years during which I seldom or never heard from you. Think of the heartlessness of your present demand, and the reasons with which you urge it. Don't talk to me! I have no patience with your selfish greed. I am determinod to do one kindly act before I die, to make the life of one person smooth. You cannot change my resolve." "Have you see this Count Arevalo ?" inquired Adlowe,, abruptly. Lord Trevelyan replied in the negative. "There is no such person, in my belief,' declared Adlowe, hotly. "This 'countess' who came here to-night is not that girl's mother. The mother is a mystery. The father is dead." "How do you know this?" demanded the mar- quis, with an astounded look. "I don't know it. I have simply guessed it," was the quick response. "Are you blind, uncle? Do you suppose that this girl's blue eyes are an accident? Do you suppose, too, that it was sim- ply by some strange freak of nature that she bears. the Trevelyan stamp- on her features? How did she come to have Geoffrey Trevelyan's strange eyes?" " I den't know," stammered the marquis, in be- wilderment. "What are you aiming at, Ormond? What is it your words imply ?" "Simply this," hissed Adlowe, fairly driven to desperation: "I believe this Giralda. Arevalo to he the daughter of your hated nephew, Geoffrey Trevelyan—born of some unknown woman before he went to the Brazils to die !"
Dord Trevelyan gave a wild, startled look at his nephew, and then silently turned aways his face, covering it with his hands. There was a brief silence between the two.

At length Adlowe said: "I was too precipitate, my load, in saying that I did not believe in the existence of a Count Are- valo. There may be such a personage, and he may have a wife and family. lt does not follow, however, that Giralda is their child. They may have adopted her, or been hired to take charge of her."

The marquis did not reply. Adlowe noticed that a strange tremor was shaking the herculean figure, and he did not venture to soon speak again. He watched the old lord for a long time in silence. Then ht moved uneasily in his chair, to attract the attention of his relative.

In this he was successful. The marquis raised his head and turned his face towards his nephew, revealing a stern, set countenance, on which the traces of a mighty emotion yet lingered. ". Adlowe,' he said, in a low voice, his eyes burning with a strange expression the younger man could not analyze, " it is barely possible that your suspicion is right ! If it were true, it would account for the mutual attraction between me and the child. Ormond, understand me fully. If Geoffrey were still living. I would pursue him like a Nemesis. I would not be satisfied until his cowardly ass ,4 s- sin's soul knew something of the tortures I have j felt. I would never rest," and the grand eyes j blazed now with terrible fires—" never ! until the law had wreaked its vengeance upon him, and he I knew himself a helpless, disgraced, outcast convict ! But, Ormond," and now a broken thrill pulsed through the concentrated voice, and the fires in the eyes were suddenly dimmed, "there was a time when his evil passions slept, and Geoffrey was an innocent boy. If Giralda were what your j strange suspicious indicate, his child, the offspring ' of that period of boyish innocence, she could not have inherited his hypocrisy and baseness. She is what he might have been. We will not discuss the question further. Whoever and whatever she may be, I will keep the child and provide for her as I have said." A malignant scowl for & moment convulsed the polished features of Lord Adlowe. It disap- peared almost immediately, but not before the Marquis had observed it. "You will excuse me for not prolonging the interview," said the latter, with dignity. " Come and see me to-morrow before we leave, or come down to the Park at any time, but leave me now, Ormond." lie leaned forward, touching the hand-bell on the table. The valet immediately made his ap- pearance, and Lord Adlowe arose and took his leave, a host of evil passions surging like an angry sea in his breast. " Sixty thousand pounds?" he muttered, as he made his way down the stairs and into the street. " The old dotard ! No man in his senses would give that sum to a girl whom he had not known a fortnigllt, and whose very existence is a mystery. I would send him to a mad-house if I could !" He hailed a hansom cab at this juncture, entered it, and was driven to his hotel. He hastened up to his own climbers with a surly face and an embittered heart.

His chamber, into which he burst abruptly, was dimly lighted and cheerless in aspect. The fire had nearly burnt itself out. His valet was .stretched on the rug before the hearth, sleeping 80510(4. Adlowe awakened him rudely by a touch with his foot, and ordered him to stir up the lire and draw the curtains. Then he sat down, gloomy and discontented. This is the la,est"complexion cure" story :—A lady had in her employ an excellent girl who had one fault —her face was always in a smudge. Her mistress tried to tell her to wash her face without offending her, and At last resorted to strategy. "Do you know, Bridget," she remarked in a confidential manner, " it is said that if you wash your face every day in hot, soapy Water, it will make you lbok beautiful 2" "Will it now 2" an- wered Bridget, looking contemplative for a moment. "Sore it's a wonder you nivver tried it yourself, mum."

Darning Stockings. There is no little skill requisite in darning stockings neatly. The mere darning up of the holes always seems a waste of tim9, as they pull apart as soon as worn. ,It is best to turn the stockings inside out, and run neatly for a little distance over the thin or worn parts around the holes, taking up on the needles as little of the sur- face as possible, so that the right side will scarcely show that the back has been run. After darning over all thin places, turn the stockings to the right side and cross the darning. Weave it in over the holes, confining the edges neatly and smoothly. If one will take time to run the heels before they are in holes it is still better, and they will last much longer.
Paid Work for Women.

An English woman of title is says " Cassell's Family ' Magazine." making a good income from table deco:w- ing. Her love for the beautiful in nature and art is put to use in the laying'of tables for luncheons and dinners, and with a few flowers and ribbons she is able to per- torm wonders. All her friends know of her talent. ani do not hesitate to employ her in preference, to a florist. Her work is now in such demand that she has engaged an assistant to help her in the less elaborate decorations. This is an employment that might well be taken up by a large number of ladies. The remuneration is at the rate of from two to four shillings an hour. I do not know whether scientific dusting is at all in vogue in London, but in most of the American cities. when,' fewer servants are employed, the work of dusting Ik' drawing, dining and best' bed-rooms is often done by an outside htlp, who, from her knowledge of the value cf handsome furniture and brie-à brae, performs her dutit, with more care than cin be expected from ignorant ser- vants. What honse-wife has mt had the experience of fitting from the mantel a vase or statuette, and having • the top or head come off in her hand in a most mira- colfius way ? Mary Ann, questioned as to the cause of the dismemberment, sometimes denies, or often boldly confesses to having knocked it, while she declares that: "It don't matter, mum. I put it on again and it's only a little thing!" Tell her that the •' little thing" cost ail the way from five tl a hundred pounds, and she will look at her mistress in amazed doubt, which plainly says: "I don't believe it t" Such ornaments placed in charge of a person of refinement and education rarely meet with these mishaps. It would pay the majority of mis- trez,ses to expend a few shillings in this way on " turn- ing-out" days and at louse cleaning time. That it it the housemaid's business to attend to the washing and dusting of brie-A-brae we shall all agree, but it is certain that she will never do it properly until she has a differ- ent home or school training from that given her at prE. sent. The care of nice furniture and ornaments is some- , thing that many gentlewomen understand intuitively, • and I would recommend that this branch of female in- dustry he given over to them. The work is neither ilifficiiit nor unpleasant, and delicately moulded hands are particularly adapted to it.

div.p: As .his lordship had expected, he was Kush, the detective. "No news yet, I suppose ? " said his lordship, moodily motioning his visitor to a seat. "It is strange how easily a woman can elude all your watchfulness, Rush." "Women are worse to track than men, my lord," responded the detective, philosophically, seating himself. "They are all full of their little arts and wiles when they are watched, but my lady beats all I ever saw. She's a remarkable woman— remarkable ! " "And that's all you have come to tell me?" asked Adlowe, disappointedly.

"No, my lord," returned the detective looking vacantly at his employer. "I have tried to get into the good graces of Mistress Mary Fleck, her ladyship's seamstress and tire-woman, since I last saw your lordship. I tried to make love to her, but she snapped me up short. I offered her money to betray her mistress' and the way she berated me wasn't slow. Talk of a pagan's devotion to his idol! 'Twon't compare with Fleck's devotion to her mistress.' _ _ .
"You have come, then Bimply to report thit failure? "

"No, my lord. It is merely incidental," and the detective's countenance grew still more vacant of expression. "1 catne to say, my lord, that I saw a lady come out of Hampton House this even- ing that I hadn't seen go in. She walked to the corner and took a cab, rode a few squares, got out, walked a couple of blocks, took another cab, and drove straight t 9 the Wiltonleigh Hotel. Stayed an hour and five minutes. Came down directly after your lordship went up the stairs. Entered cab, and went back to Hampton House same way as she had come. Very clever woman, whoever she was. Is there such an inmate of the Hampton family ? " "No. Describe her," cried Adlowe, excitedly. "Tall, stout, with thick black vail, old-fash- ioned bonnett, and two long, yellow curies. Dressed in black silk. Seemed to be a respectable old dowager." "It is the same woman," ejaculated Lord Ad- lowe, with increasing excitement. "She went to call on my uncle, Lord Trevelyan. She is the Countess of Arevalo, an actress, or pretended ac- tress."

"Never heard the name," said the detective. ". If you know her, its all right, my lord. Of course the Lady Beatrice Hampton would not disguise herself to go and call on a nobleman that she knew well. My error arose from excess of zeal—" "Let us first see that you have erred in follow- ing this woman from Hampton House," interrupted Adlowe, rising, and pacing the floor. "I never saw her till to-night. My uncle really knows nothing of her. There came to my uncle only last week, in answer to an advertisement for a com- panion, a beautiful young girl, the image of my dead cousin, Geoffrey Trevelyan. He brought this girl up to London with. him. .Her resemblance to Geoffrey, whom he once loved as much as he now hates his memory, has made a strong impression upon him. He is going to make a will, leaving her a handsome fortune, to-morrow. He has seen none of her relatives save this pretended or real countess. The countess appeared to-night to con- sent to the adoption of her child by the marquis. My idea is, Rush, that this girl has not Geoiliey's eyes and the Trevelyan features without reason." The detective looked like,a bloodhound when he scents his prey. " Why has the Lady Beatrice never married ? " continued Adlowe, hurrying in his walk. " Was the secretly married to Geoffrey before he fled? There was plenty of time for a marriage by license after my cousin was expelled from the Park. Is this girl the oMpring of that secret union? " _

"The theory is plausible," said the detective. "It is more than plausible. What more natural than such a course? Oh I have been blind !" and his lordship raged to and fro. " The girl is their child—the child of the Lady Beatrice and Geoffrey Trevelyan. She was sent to the Park to win the old man's heart and his savings."

"If the young lady is the daughter of the late Geoffrey Trevelyan," observed the detective, "she is the rightful heir of the Trevelyan es- tates." Lord Adlowe reeled as if he had been- shot. "So she is !" he faltered, his face becoming pale to ghastliness. "I—i must be deceived. I have alarmed myself unnecessarily. Yet,, Rush, I wish you would institute a search of the church regis- ters at the West Eud. Look sharply for the record of such a marriage in the registers of 1850. Spare no pains, time, or money. 1. will pay liberally for everything." He sat down, trembling:. "It is by no means certain," he said, as if reassuring himself, after a pause, "that the countess was the Lady Beatrice disguised. My anxieties make me tearfully suspicious. There May be really a Countess Arevalo, and she may know the Lady Beatrice Hampton, although the countess is said to be an actress. I. will know the truth to- morrow," and he shut his teeth firmly together. "One thing is proven to my satisfaction,: There is some mysterious connection between the Lady Beatrice and Miss Arevalo. It could scarcely have been Miss Arevalu's strange resemblance to the dead Geoffrey Trevelyan that made her ladyship faint. And yet it is barely possible. I shall hasten my marriage with the Lady Beatrice," he added, "and acquire the right to know all her secrets. I will not daily along in this manner. I will be no longer played with. I know and sus- pected enough," and his lordship's brow knotted themselves together darkly, " to make me a dan- gerous and terrible enemy. I will give the Lady Beatrice a chance to secure me as a friend and ally. She will not dare again to refuse me."' _ .

These threats were muttered under his breath, and neither the detective nor the valet compre- hended their import. "The mysterious absences of the Lady Beatrice from her home, her persistent celibacy, her secrec in going and. -coming from Hampton House," re- marked the detective, thoughtfully, "all point to interests outside of her own proper home. If Geoffrey Trevelyan were still living—if she were his wife—if this young girl were their child, I could understand why the young lady has been sent to Trevelyan Park. If we go on the ground that Mr. Geoffrey is dead, and that there was a secret marriage between him and the Lady Beatrice, then this Miss Arevalo is the offspring of that secret marriage. The absences of her ladyship were to visit this child, whom. she dare not acknowledge as her own, because of the infamy covering the father's name. I incline to the latter theory.' "So do It." said his lordship, speaking as by a painful effort. "And this Countess of Arevalo ? " "Is the foster-mother of the giri." "No, no!" cried Lord Adlowe, a sudden and great agitation convulsing him as a strange con- vulsion forced itself on his soul with the swiftness of a flash. "That hand—l remember it now The Countess of Arevalo is the girl's mother! The Countess of Arevalo is the Lady Beatrice Hampton cleverly disguised!" He covered his pale face, trembling and panic- stricken.

div.head: SEED WAS 3,000 YEARS OLD.
div.p: THE SEED WAS 3,000 YEARS OLD.

"If I should take this to America and sow it near my home, I wonder if it would grow there !" Who said this, and what was lie talking about ? That is what you want to know. The man who said it waS =.n American explorer in Egypt about fifteen years ago. fie was speaking of a handful of wheat he had found in a tomb whic!i had never before been opened. lie took the wheat to his own country, sowed it in the Mississippi Valley, and it sprang up beautifully. He re-sowed the product, and so kept on doing until at last he had a crop of several acres of Egyptian wheat. The wonder is in this—that the original handful had lain in the dark- ness of the tomb, on a stone slab, for over 3,000 years. Well, then. What does that amount to ? It a mountS to this. It shows how long the principle of lile Will remain after you fancy it is gone. The seeds of both good and evil are hard to kill. Here's an illustration of of a different sort, but quite as important.

Twenty-six years ago, Mrs. Ann Copping, now living in London, W 45 ccgk in a gentleman's family at The Terrace, Champion Hill. At that time she was one day attacked with sciatica and lumbago. teitS early as five o'clock on Saturday morning, the bl!tral Station at Warrington presented an ani- k;rd appearance, due to the departure of about Persons by Messrs. P. Walker and Son's annual I:tUrsion to York and Scarborough. The "trippers" kere accommodu.ted in two trains, and punctually tairt,ile appointed times the trains steamed out of the "nn. The journey to Scarborough—for very few desirious of breaking the journey at the fine city York—is a very long one, perhaps too long for a Ira excursion. In order to reach the place of (Joanna• it was necessary to proceed along four different M' Way c.nnecnons, viz.: The C.L.C. M.S. and L., 41:„Tand, and the Great Northern, the distance being ot ut 150 miles. Beantlul scenery surrounded the line oakute, more especially fn Derbyshire and Yorkshire. approaching Scarborough, the scenery around, at e gives the visitor a pleasing impression, the district R,„:11g 'well wooded and hilly. The first train arrived in 17:11torough at 9.30., thus completing the journey in sa.tistactory time of 4 hours. The Warrington teelunteer band accompanied the excursion, and played /eral selections at the various stopping placrs,and also t:talded the arrival ot the Warrington " trippers " to the it akients of Scarborough. Whilst speaking of the hand *Atnay be stated that during the day two performances kcre given by it at the Feople'e Palace and Aquarium. thr• Armstrong was the conductor, and the playing of ,o:„band was favourably commente:i upon by visitors. thp'ing to the foreshore, after the necessary walk Fllgh the town from the railway stanon, the appear- thee is disappointing. One does not expect to find facing Promenade and in the centre of a fine bay, at a tt liar watering place like Scarborough, a number of houses, fiddling shops, and advertisement spaces, eannounced "To let." There is of course on the tie''Rtit hand side Gf the bay, the South Cliff, with its Spa 0 at to, and on the left an historic castle, towering high a f 1,44 oreland which divides the north and south bays, aires Scarborough the happy possessor of two or inlets of the sea. It is the north bay—a watering thfe of itself—and more modern in appearance than kre' °lle mentioned, that adds beauty to the town. Here fino drive and pier, with a more imposing prom- in striking contrast with the narrow streets, and i..gniarly built houses in other parts of the town.which ;:tes it a combination of both new and old. The ex- It'roionists made their way to the most interesting spots Wt!:lacl around the town, and some procee,led as far as op ItbY, and others to Filey. Beautifully fine weather thevitiled throughout the day. Soon after eight o'clock, %tB„Warringtofl "trippers" were at the station again,and th 4.p. they were all entrained and on their way back to otets good old town." The first train was in charge (Xincillor Baird and Mr. PAter. Mr. Fulton Smith to,ttllargehf the second train. div.head: MISSION.
div.p: MISSION.
PICNIC TO MANLEY.

A picnic, organised by the members o 7 the Gospel Temperance Mission, was held on Monday. to Manley. This place, which is comparatively unknown, but which is a most beautiful spot, is situated on the confines of Delamere Forest, and is about seven or eight miles from Chester. A start was made at about 8.15 a.m., when the party num- bering 22 left, the Mission Hall, Buttermarket-at., in one of Mr. Connor's 'buses, and proceeded along Chester-road, through Daresbury, Preston Brook, Sutton Weaver and Fr odsbam. The Chester main road was left a mile beyond Frodsham, when the Tarvin-road was taken. The first place of any importance to be reached was silvanley, a quaint old village, which contains a quaint old church. After leaving Al vanley,human habitations were few and far between for some miles. The scenery at. this part of the journey was beautiful, and w•quld not discredit even Wales. The roads, however,were not intended for quick travelling, for at one time, the horses were nulling might and main to get up the hill, and immediately afterwards, the brakes had to be applied to keep the 'bus from overrunning the horses. " Get out a..d walk," was a very com- mon order. Pendie Hill was a very prom- inent landmark, for it was covered with trees from summit to base. The road led round the base of this hill, and immediately afterwards Manley was reached, where the horses and 'bus were put up. Dinner was partaken of at Manley Post Office, after which the various places of interest were visited. A visit was paid to Ash- ton Hall, near the village of Ashton Beyes. The road led through Mouldsworth, which is a very pretty village. Permission was obtained to go through the beautiful gardens around Ashton nil, and many were the expressions of admiration at the sights that were to be seen. The hothouses were filled with fruit, but as it was all "sour," they were left severely alone. The grounds abounded with rabbit warrens, and the fields literally teemed with these little rodents. It was now getting tea time, but Mr. Drury could tot resist the temptation of holding an impromptu service at the little Wes- leyan Chapel at Mouldsworth. A hearty tea was partaken of at Manley, and time for returning soon arrived. The return journey was made by a slightly different route, and some extensive views could be taken of the eounty round. At one spot, away in the distance, could be seen the broad estuary of the Mersey, dotted with craft of various kinds,while in another direction the country round Chester and right away in North Wales, and as far as Snowdon could be seen. The Chester road was joined a little below Frsdsham, after a most precipitous descent from the hills during, which a number of the party endeavoured to strike up a tune some- thing about being "in the lifeboat," but everyone was thinking that being "in the 'bus," was bad enough on that steep road, let alone the lifeboat. The journey from Frodsham to Warrington was without incident, and the "good old town "war. reached about 9.30 p.m. everyone being extremely satisfied with the day's outing. The arrangements were in the hands of Mr. A. Horrocks, and be very efficiently performed his duties.

div.head: WIDNES TOWN COUNCIL.
div.p: WIDNES TOWN COUNCIL.

The monthly meeting of this council was held in the Boardroom, Town Hall, on Tuesday afrernoon. The following were present: Aldermen Sadler, Tim- mis, Williamson,and Wareing; Councillors Bullough Wright, Go-sage, Smith, Hodgkinson, Owens, O'Donnell, Quinn, Davies, Gough, Singletun,C,trney, and Shuttleworth ; Messrs. H. S. Oppenheim (town clerk), Craik (deputy town clerk). Hoyle (account- ant), Carr (engineer), Sinclair (surveyor), Lowe (nuisance inspector) ; and Dr. Oliaele (medical officer). In the absence of the Mayor, the deputy mayor, (Alderman Sadler),occupied the chair.

div.head: HIGHWAY COMMITTEE.
div.p: HIGHWAY COMMITTEE.

A meeting of this committee was held on the 28:h June. The Town Clerk reported that the action Broome v. Corporation had been heard in the Widnes County Court OA the 22nd June, and that judgment had since been given in favour of the plaintiff to the n mount of £3O and costs.—The Town Clerk was instructed to give notice of appeal.Councillors Quinn and Hodgkinson moved the adoption of the minutes. —Councillor Smith wished to know how soon the Committee would be prepared to carry out the making of back passages &c., as per a for- mer resolution. Also whether any steps were being taken by the committee as to the dangerous wall in front of Mersey View.--Councillor Quinn in reply said the back passages in West Bank would be immediately pro- ceeded with when they had the powers for borrowing. The other question would be inquired into.—The min- utes were passed.

div.head: IIEAI.TI3 COMMITTEE.
div.p: IIEAI.TI3 COMMITTEE.

A Meeting of this committee was held on the 29Lh June. A letter, dated 7th June, from Mr. Frederick A. Jones, deputy coroner, was read, stating that at a re- cent inquest the jury had made a presentment that it was desirable that a mortuary should be provided by the Corporation, and r(questing him to bring the mat. ter before the local authority. It was resolved that the letter be referred to the borough sury ever to report upon. Number of patients in Infectious Diseases Hos- pital at last meeting was nil ; admitted since, 1 ; still in, 1. Number of patients in Accident Hospital at last meeting, 7 ; admitted since, 5 ; discharged, 5 ; died, 1; patients still in, 8. The Medical Officer of Health re- ported that during the month the births had been 76, equal to 30-4 per 1,000; deaths, 37, equal to 14-8 per 1.000. The cases ot infectious diseases notified were 43. The death rate was considered satisfactory, being similar to that of last month, viz.. 14-8 per thousand. Scarlatina continued to be prevalent. All the cases were of a very mild type, and had been treated successfully at their own homes. There had been five cases of typhoid fever notified this month, but it was not considered necessary to have any removed to the hoipital. On the motion of Councillors Wright and Smith, the minutes were adopted.

div.head: OAS AND WATER COMMITTEE.
div.p: OAS AND WATER COMMITTEE.

This committee reported that tests of the gas made by Mr. C. E. Bellamy, of Liverpool, on the 11th and 29th ult., read as follows: Illuminating pcwer, 18.71 arid 19.57 candles respectivelv.—The Surveyor reported that the erection of the pavilion was now practically com- plete,and the painting awl glazing which was now in hand was expected to be finished this week. The furniture had been delivered and the premises would be ready for ' use on Thursday, the 12:h inst. The amount of land levelled now amounted to 4,500 square yards.—lt was resolved that the scale of charges for the use of the pavilion, Sicc., at Pex Hill, now submitted and revised by the committee, be approved and adopted, and that the engineer be authorised and empowered to deal with applications for the use of the pavilion and ground on behalf of the committee.—lt was also resolved that advertisements be inserted in the local Tapers announc- ing that the pavilion and grounds were now open to the public upon the terms approved by the committee. The price of coke to ordidary consumers was reduced tz, 6d. per ton.—On the motion of Alderman Timmis and Councillor Bullough the minutes were adopted.

div.head: GENERAL PURPOSES AND PARLIAMENTARY COMMITTEE

div.head: IHE EXAMiNER, SATURDAY, JULY 14, 1894.
div.p: IHE EXAMiNER, SATURDAY, JULY 14, 1894.
WARRINGTON JUVENILE RECHABITES.

A conference ol juvenile workers in the Warring- ton Juvenile District was held on Saturday after- noon in John Dimond Juvenile Tent room, Cairo- street, Warrington Invitations were sent out to surrounding districts. M anchester, Liverpool, Runcorn, Frodsham and Preston Brook supplied representativ€l3, to some of which the Warrington District is indebted for very able, instructive and encouraging remarks. Bro. Fred. W. Brett, H.S.J.T. presided at the (3:inference. and in his ai!dress gase some excellent and very practical suggestions as to how juvenile tents ought to be worked. Tea was provided at six o'clock At 7.30 a public meeting was held and presided over by Councillor H.Roberts, J.P. lii the course of his remarks the chairman said it was a pleasure to him to be associated with any meeting that had for its object the promotion of the great cause of Temperance. With regard to juvenile work he pointed out that it had been said ty wise men that if only the children of the country were trained to right habits until their brain power had been sufficiently developed to enable them to see for themselves the righteousness of those habits, the future of the country was safe. Tho one difficulty more than another that was an obstacle to improvement was the drink traffic, and the responsibility rested upon all of them to see that the children were educated so as to avoid the evils 'of this traffic. The circumstances that had occurred in Warrington during the last few years showed that it was necessary for men to take a stand upon this question. There were cases continually coming before the Police Court directly or indirectly through drink, and when a publican was, brought up for wilfully breaking the law it was a m(,st difficult thing to obtain a conviction against him. He was sympatbizA with as if he possessed all the virtues and as if it was a. shame Oaf.. the law should be put in force against him. If a man broke the law whether he be a publican or sinner of any other kind, he ought to be punished. (Hear. hear.) The speakers were Messrs. Fred. W. Brett, H.S.J.T., of Cardiff, H. J. Jones, Man- chester dis. treas., and Miss Bessie Dutton, of Moore. On Sundly afternoon, .Bro. Brett gave a very instructive address to the scholars of Brick-street Mission Sunday school, and on Sunday night addressed a large out-door meeting in connection with the Gospel Temperance Mission at the end of Bewsey-street.

Mr. Brandreth submitted the report of the Finance Committee. The accounts for payment included £6 7s. from the Runcorn Improvement Commissioners. This sum was for the maintenance in hospital and expenses of burial of John Sims, who was removed to the hospital from the schooner " Lizzie" when suffering from typhoid fever and who died from the effects on the 26th June. The account was for seven days' maintenance, £1 1O.; cost of removal 16s. 61.; hearse 17s. 61. ; and coffin £3 3s. There was also an account from the Runcorn Burial Board for 13a. 6,1., amount of fees.—Mr. Bran- dreth thought the charges' were heavy.—The Clerk said that the man was removed by the Sanitary Authority and with reeard to the coffin, men had had to work all night to make it in order that the body might be en- closed in it the next morning. He also went into fur- ther explanations of the other items, and in answer to Mr. Bra ndreth said that he understood from the captain of the " Lizzie" that £1 was due to Sims, and the cap- tain had promised to do what he could towards repay- ing the Authority.—After a little further discussion the subject dropped.

div.head: ANNIVERSARY OF THE HALTON FEMALE FRIENDLY SOCIE ry.
div.p: ANNIVERSARY OF THE HALTON FEMALE FRIENDLY SOCIE ry.

On Monday the members of the above society celebrated their 78th anniversary amid the usual manifestations of rejoicing. The event arouses so much interest in the surrounding district that many hundreds of people were in the village at noon to witness the procession. At about two o'clock the members assembled in the church schoolroom, and subsequently proceeded to the church where a short ser- vice was conducted by the vicar, the Rev. G. D. Wray, in the absence of the Rev. Canon Greenall, of Grappen- hall. The service over, the procession numbering about ' 200 was again formed, and paraded the village, headed by the Runcorn town and district band, (conducted by Mr. T. Woods), Lady Brooke, Mrs. H. Reynolds, Mrs. Wray, the Rev. G. D. Wray, the Rev. S. Wilkinson, (vicar of Timperley), Mr. Charles Reynolds, Mr. John Henry Gamon' and Mr. T. Wright. Later on they con- gregated in a large marquee at Halton Castle and en- joyed a capital tea. The after proceedings were presided over by Lady Brooke, president of the society. In an address to the members she said it gave her great pleasure to be with them, and hoped that has time went on their numbers would increase. She loyked upon the society as a stand- ing proof of the kindly feeling and sympathy which had existed for so many years between the Brooke family and the residents of Halton. She trusted that that feel- ing would ever continue, and that the benefits of the club might always be extended to those who were in need of them. The record of the club, judging from the accumulated funds, was a very good one,and they must surely all feel gratified by the prosperity which attended it. They gratefully acknowledged that this prosperity was in a large measure due to the devotion ability and tact with which Mr. C. Reynolds had managed the affairs, and she was convinced that she would only be I expressing the feelings of those present if she said that I the club was most fortunate in possessing a trustee so able, willing, and energetic. (Applause.) She also ex- pressed satisfaction a the restoration to health of Dr. I Carruthers, aud congratulated him upon his marriage. The club had already done this by the presentation they made him on the occasion of his wedding. (Applause.) Her ladyship concluded by hoping that all would spend a very pleasant evening. The Rev, S. Wilkinson, in a short address, proposed a vote of thanks to Lady Brooke for her attendance, which was heartily accorded. The Rev. G. D. Wray then maved a vote ot thanks to the trustees, Messrs. Charles Reynolds and J. H. Gamon. This was passed with en- thusiasm.

Mr. Reynolds, in responding, thanked them for the kind m inner in which their services had been recognized. He had been closely connected with the society for 20 years, and during that period he had only been absent on one occasion when the anniversaries were held. Lady Brooke had correctly stated that the affairs were in a prosperous condition, and he doubted whether there Was another society in the country whose financial position was so satisfactory. (Applause.) Practically the funds had been doubled during the past 20 years, and if this went on they might hope that at the next quinquennial valuation the club would oecupy a stronger position than it had ever done. The thing they viewed with a certain amount of dread, however, was the increase of the sick pay. Previously they had paid so little in the summer that their receipts had enabled them to go through the winter without debt. Now, however, they were paying. £3 3A. per week in the middle of the summer. He hoped Iloilo of the members would apply for sick pay except when it was absolutely necessary, as it was this which was the crucial test of any society. He had the pro- spectus of a proposed new club for ladies in that dis- trict, issued by the Order of Oddfellows, for certain benefits on certain conditions and graduated payments. The fee was from 16 to 18 years is. 4d. per month,2o to 25 years is. per year extra, for every two years above that augmented is., and at 45 years 2s. per month, which was about 275. per year. He did not think the 1, male club need have any fear of its position, for he bought it would hold its own with any that might be started in the district. . . . .

Mrs. Booth thought that persons entering the club be- tween the ages of 21 and 25 should be charged an addi- tional is. per annum to the present fees. Also that the district of the society should be extended.—Mr. Reynolds said that the matter should receive every consideration at the next meeting.—Mr. Gamon also responded to the vote of thanks saying that the questions raised were of importance and deserved the most careful attention. He was convinced that the trustees and officers would al- ways devote their energies to the welfare of the society. Their secretary, Mr. Wright, had received a letter from Dr. Carruthers who expressed his regret at not being able to be present, but hoped the gathering would be a Qreat sucdess. The following ladies and gentlemen were likewise accorded votes of thanks :—Mrs. Wray, and Mrs. Henry R-1-nolds, Drs. Carruthers, Ormsby, MacLennan, and Robinson, the Rev. G. D. Wray,, and Mr. Wright, secretary. Dancing was afterwards indulged in on the green con- nectel with the Halton Castle Hotel, the Runcorn Tc,wn and District Band accompanying.

div.head: GAMBLE INSTITUTE, ST. HELENS.
div.p: THE GAMBLE INSTITUTE, ST. HELENS.
THE PLANS PASSED.

The preliminary arrangements in connection with the work of erecting the Gamble Institute, St, Helens, were advanced another step on Wednesday when the plans were submitted for approval to the health Committee of the St. Helens Corporation. Mt. John Forster presided, and there were also present Alderman J. C. Gamble, Messrs. Burt, Burchall, and Massey.—The Borough Surveyor (Mr. Boom) said the plan: were all correct, and they were approved.—The blois, which were submitted by Messrs. Briggs and Wolstenholme, aichitscts, of Blackburn, showed a three- storey building and basement, with a frontage and main ent ranee to Hardshaw-street. The ground floor will be used as the free library portion of the building. The entrance will communicate with a spacious hall, behind which will be t h.. lending department. The whole of the whole of the fr;ntage to Bickerstaff-street will be occu- pied by the newsroom, while on the opposite wing there will be the reference library and bays and girls reading- r,..oms. Time basement floor will be devoted to the manuel tramming room, building classroom, metallurgical labora- ory, plumbing classroom, and engineering laboratory. The first floor will cemtain classrooms, &c., for the. vari- ous branches of technical education, and the second floor will be devoted entirely to the chemical and arts depart- ments. The building will be faced externally with red- pressed bricks and terracotta, arid, will, when corn- p'eted, form a very handsome structure. Already work has been commenced, and the site is being prepared for the foundations and basement.

div.head: THINGS HEARD AND SEEN AT WARRINGTON
div.p: THINGS HEARD AND SEEN AT WARRINGTON

Daring the usual summer vacation of the elemen- tary day school scholars in the town, I notice that several alterations are being carried out in connec- tion with some of the schools. These are being done at the instigation of the Education Depart- ment. That wicked Mr. Acland in his endeavours to provide healthy schools for the benefit of the children has given special instructions to the in- spectors to examine schools, and report on their sanitary condition. The alterations now being made to schools in the town are tie results of reports made at the time of the examinations last October. Managers of voluntary schools take, more or less, unkindly to these suggested improvements, and ' some have not been slow to say that it means forc- ing a School Board. These gentlemen, as a rule, have merely just looked after the government grant, and left such things as dingy classrooms, worn-out and out-of-date school furniture, insani- tary drains, and improper ventilation to take take of themselves. But now that these defects are being pointed out to them, with the stipulation that they must be carried out, on peril of losing the grant, managers are almost at their wits end to know where the money is to come from.

From the report on the Technical Institute for 1892-3 which has just been issued, I gather that the number of students who attended the School of Art and School of Science during that session was 545, which unfortunately shows a decrease on the pre- vious year. Sixty classes met weekly under the charge of 23 teachers. Mention is made of the highly creditable action of the Warrington Co- operative Society in paying the fees, wholly or in part, of no fewer than 100 of these students. The example set by the Co-operative Society is one worthy of emulation, particularly by local em- ployers of labour who take any interest in the advancement of education amongst their young employes. The results of the examinations in both schools were very satisfactory, and in the School of Art, especially, notwithstanding the fact that the art students numbered almost 100 fewer than the previous year, the number of passes actually ex- ceeded that of the previous session.

As will be seen from the following paragraph which I extract from the report alluded to above, teachers in the School of Science work under many difficulties. "The conditions under which the claQses of the School of Science are carried on in scattered rooms in four different buildings, most of which are ill adapted and can only be temporarily used for the purpose, cannot but be detrimental to the work of the school, not to speak of the incon, venience to students and teachers,and the resulting difficulties of oversight and management. The Committee considers that if the School of Science is to make satisfactory progress a building must shortly be erected, properly equipped according to modern ideas,and suited to the special requirements of the town." The balance sheet for the year end- ing 31st August, 1893, shows that the committee commenced with a balance in hand of ..E26 12s. 4d., and finished the year with a balance overdrawn of £295 15s.

Judging by the Warrington police reports, the town has within its borders a good number of pugnacious women. Rarely a week passes but some woman appears before the bench with most inglorious black eyes, which she has received at the hands of one of her feminine neighbours. Or per- haps she is able to produce a nice little bundle of hair which has been forcibly extracted from her head, during a melee which has taken place owing to some dispute about the return of Mrs. So-and-So's clothes prop. It is said that these lively variations in otherwise rather monotonous lives are largely due to the gossiping propensities of the parties concerned, and, therefore, it often happens that the Bench find that both parties are to blame, and the complainant and defendant gener- ally leave the court without any conviction having been recorded, whilst the sore of ill-feeling is often considerably worse than before. div.head: WARRINGTON MANUFACTURERS AND THE 3SIANCHESTER SHIP CANAL.
div.p: WARRINGTON MANUFACTURERS AND THE 3SIANCHESTER SHIP CANAL.
A PROTEST.

The following report has been sent us with a request that we should publish it: Last .week, a number of ratepayers of Warrington met together at the residence of one of the party, for the purpose of considering the pro- posed terms of settlement of the action brought by Messrs. Fairclough and Sons against the Manches- ter Ship Canal Company. It was pointed out that a meeting had been held at the offices af Messrs. Greenall, and Buckton, which purported to repre- sent the opinions of the manufacturers and traders of the town. The opinion was expressed that that meeting could not be held to represent the general opinion of the manufacturers of Warrington, inas- much as no circular was received by a large num- ber of them, and in order to make such an opinion valuable, this _step ought to have been taken.

-A. large s-ection-of the manufacturers of Warring- ton feel increasing alarm at the way in which their interests have been dealt with by the Corporation of Warrington, The Canal has now been opened for over six months, and yet. notwithstanding that fact, thousands upon thousands of tons of goods which the Ship Canal Company might receive the benefit of, and which on account of the cheaper rates on the canal would effect the ratepayers a considerable saving, are allowed to go through the old channels of traffic. It was the opinion of the meeting that a great deal too much was beir,g made of the river, whilst those manufacturers who were not situated on the river w're made to acquiesce no/ens volens in what seemed to be a determined effort to lolackball the Manchester Ship Canal. They therefore fervently hoped that the directors of the Manchester Ship Canal Company would take notice of this action, and not be guided by a party I'whik posed as the representative of the general tAkiblic opinion of Warrington. The Manchester Ship Canal meant a good deal more than the half tide docks to the traders of Liverpool, because at high tide, the Eastham locks being open, vessels could sail up to Warrington, without having to wait, a.. they did in the case of the half tide docks, for suffi- cient water to enable the vessels to pass over the dock sills. It was also further pointed out that there was no quay on the river at which the gen- eral traders oi Warrington could load and unload their cargoes, and that if the Corporation really had the interest of the manufacturers and traders of Warring ton at heart, this would be one of the ver first things they would wish to see supplied.

div.head: HINTON BITP.IAL GROUND.
div.p: THE HINTON BITP.IAL GROUND.

The CLERK said that he had rLceived a communication from the Catholic priest of Rixt on, to the effect that the plot assigned to the Catholics in Rixton burial grouni was not large enough, and alzzo wishing to have a plot separate from the other denominations.—Mr. BEATON said that the question had been so. tied, and it would not be wise to re-open it, as other denominations had as much right to ask to have alterations as the Catholics. Alter a lengthy discussion,it was decided that the Clerk see the priest and endeavour to come to some amicable arrangement, and report to the next meeting of the Board.

On the motion of Mr. A. JOLLEY, seconded by Mr. W. LONG, James Arstall was appointed sexton and care- taker to the cemetery, the :,aidry to be decided by a committee formed of the chairman, the clerk, and the surveyor. MEDICAL OFFICER'S REPORT.

The Medical Officer reported that thete had been 39 births and 17 deaths during tie past month, the death rate being 14•6 per 1,000, 34,.ain,t 14 3 the corresponding month of last year. The deaths from zymotic diseases was equal to 3 4 per I,ooo,agamst 2.6 during the correi- pending period of last year. SURVEYoII'S REPORT.

During the month, inspections had been made of the Ship Canal Company's liou!ezi, Grappenhall, Mr. Hind- ley's houses, Padgate, Mr. Bywater' s houses, Padgate, Was Tinsley's houses, Penkeili, and the Collins Greet. Colliery Company's houses, Burtonwood. Certificates of habitation were granted to the Ship Canal for two house- at Grappenhall, and Mr. Gould for house at Great Sankey.

div.head: PADGATE WATER SUPPLY.
div.p: PADGATE WATER SUPPLY.

At a meeting of the Streets Committee held on June 23, the Town Clerk of Warrington attended for the con- sideration of the water question with the Committee The Town Clerk showed that the total estimate of thi- Corporation for carrying water into Padgate was £l,OOO inasmuch as it was requisite to carry an Bin. main from Gorsey-lane to Padgate Bridge for an adequate supply, and from thence it was proposed to continue a 6in. main to the corner cc Fearnhead-line, but the Corporation proposed that ti, rest of the B.n. main from Gorsey-lane to Padgate Bridg\ and the difference between a 6in and 3m, main from Finger Post-lane over the railway bridge to Fearnhea.d-lane should fall upon themselves, these amounting to about £4oo,mAking the net cost, the inter- est upon which the Authority was asked to guarantee £6OO, which at 81 per cent. would be £5l per annum. l'he Town Clerk pointed out that the Corporation dio not wish the Authority to take the fi4ures from the estimate, but upon the actual cost which it was anticip- ated would be somewhat less. After consideration the Committee decided to recommend the Authority tn guar- antee 81 per cent. per annum on tie actual cost of a 61n. main from Padgate Bridge to Finger Post-lane,and a 3m. main from thence to Fearnhead-lane on the condition that the Corporation lay a 61n main for the whole of the dis- tance.—Toe recommendations of the Committee were adopted on the motion of Mr. A Jolley, seconded by Mr. W. Long.

THE ORFORD WATER SUPPLY. Respecting the Orford water supply, the Streets Com- mittee pointed out that the works already completed had been somewhat less than anticipated, and it was Considered that it would be best to have a similar guar- antee to that proposed in the case of Padgate, operating in Orford. After consideration the committee decided to recommend that the present agreement with the Corporation to guarantee 35 perannum be rescinded and that the Authoritv undertake to guarantee 81 per cer on the actual cost of the mains already laid up tr schools. and 84- per cent on the cost of a 3m. ma' Long-!ane and in continuation of the presr Orford-line.—The recommend motion of Mr. A. THERE are some things which are A Big Strike. done better in England than in _ _

America, and one of these is the management of a strike. A strike is a strike in England ; in America it is a " labour war." The differences seem to be due, for the most part, to two causes. In the first place the labour associa- tions of the United States are neither so firmly established nor so efficiently officered as the trades unions of England. In the. second place, and in spite of the proud boast that the States are in an unusual degree "the land of the free," the work- ing-classes are there much less protected by the law from the oppression of powerful and unscrup- ulous employers than they are in England. In industrial affairs, the huge corporations and " trusts," which are generally controlled by a few enormously wealthy capitalists, can apparently exercise a despotism of the most exasperating character, and when an emergency arises they have a ready command of all the resources of the States. The present railway troubles illustrate the situation clearly enough. The dispute origin- ally arose through a reduction of the wages of their workmen by the Pullman Palace Car Company. at the head of which is the well-known millionaire, Mr. PULLMAN. The workmen naturally demurred to this demand and asked that the matter should be submitted to arbitration, but Mr. PULLMAN peremptorily deOined • to have anything to do with conciliatory methods. His men therefore came out on strike, and as an attempt was made to stop the running of Pullman cars one railway after another was " tied up." This, of course, quickly led to a serious development of affairs, , for the United States is a country of long dis- tances and is largely dependent upon the railways for inter-communications. President CLEVELAND, as chief of the executive, thereupon decided to take action to end a condition of things which was rapidly becoming intolerable. He made a Personal appeal to MT. PULLMAN to submit the disputs with his workmen to arbitra- tion, but, although this appeal was, it is said, supported by the fifty mayors. of fifty towns, it was rejected by Mr. PULLMAN. There was clearly no hope of peace from that quarter, and as a millionaire appears to be the most sacred pro- duct of the State, there has been, of course, no
