div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JULY 14, 1894.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JULY 14, 1894.

Iwhisper of compul&on so far as the employer is concerned. With the workmen sterner measures werAdopted. Some of the strike leaders have been arrested, and are, it is said, to be prosecuted ' for conspiracy. The whole available force of Federal troops and militia were concentrated in the strike areas, and these troops have not hesi- tated to shoot. It is now declared that the "back of the strike is broken," and this is probably the case. Dissatisfied as are great masses of workpeo- ple in the United States, they are not prepared to enter upon a civil war, and this is what an organised opposition to the Federal troops would moan. At the same time is is quite clear that the time has now come for some • extensive reforms. The industrial policy of the States has been too long dominated by a class of capitalists whose single aim has been to amass wealth. In the face of the disorders which were breaking out in many directions President CLEVELAND probably had no other alternative than to practically proclaim martial lawin Chicago. But a "state of siege "is not a form of government that can subsist along with representative government, and he will be well advised if, after the Gatlings and Winchesters have repressed riot and pillage, he turns his attention to propounding a suitable remedy for the grievances of the workmen. That there are grievances of a very serious nature is clearly demonstrated by a succession of labour troubles. There is a very serious warning, too, in the fact that in some of the States public opinion has been unreservedly on the side of the strikers. When the :Militia refuse to act, haid appear to be almost ready to turn their arms against constituted authority, there is a pressing necessity for those in high places to show the wisdom of real states- men.

ACCORDING to a statement made The Deputation in the Town Council at its last Question. meeting -.Q400 a year is the sum abstracted from the Warrington Corporation ex- chequer to defray the expenses of deputations. If that be so it can hardly be said that the discussion which took place on tilt, subject was either prema- ture or uncalled for. The immediate cause of the debate was a proposal by the School Attendance Committee that a deputatioß of seven should visit the "Clio," a reformatory ship to which a number of Warrington lads have been sent. Obje.ction was taken to the number of" deputators " that it was proposed to send and in the end they were reduced by two. In the course of the debate the rather drastic suggestion was made that members of deputations should pay their own expenses. It is needless to say that this proposal did not meet with much support. Nor is there any reason why it. should. If deputations are necessary it is certainly necessary that the Corporation should pay the expenses, or otherwise the poorer members would be seriously hindered in the performance of their duties. And probably there are few people who know anything about the multifarious work that falls upon a Corporation who will argue that deputations are not needed sometimes. On the present occasion, for example, there was unquestionable force in the arguments used by Mr. SHAW GREEN, the Chair- man of the School Attendance Committee. This Committee undertakes the serious responsibility of asking the magistrates to commit refractory or neglected juveniles to the reformatory ship, and having done this they are looked to, both by the parents and the public, .to maintain a suitable. oversigh ef the young people. No doubt a visit to the "Clio" at the present time of the year partakes largely of the nature of a holiday trip, but the members of the Conr.aitteo might on this point silence their detractors by paying a visit in the depth of winter. This would answer the double purpose of displaying the stern sense of duty by which they were animated, and of seeing life on the "Clio " under the rig- ours of frost and snow. It would also probably relieve them of any necessity to select the members of the deputation by ballot, and of the temptation to make them too numer- ous. On the general question of deputations, Councillor ROBERTS undoubtedly put the whole matter in a nutshell when he discriminated between deputations which would answer some useful purpose and those which were merely got. up for the sake of a "spree." The latter kind of deputations should be rigidly discouraged,and we are, persuaded that there have been some of them if it be correct that £4OO has been spent in no year.

THE Tories are seriously disap- TheAttrciiffe Election. pointed at the result of the Atter- cliffe election. And, it must be conceded, they have some reason for their chag- rin. They had built large hopes upon the fact that three candidates were run for one seat,: and they did not disguise their elation at the pros- pect of Mr. HILL SMITH slipping in through the divisions between Liberalism and " Labourism." However, not only has Mr. HILL SMITH been soundly beaten by the Liberal candidate, but, in addition, an analysis of the poll is,in another way, causing them not a little uneasiness. They have been calculating that the running of Indepen- dent • Labour candidates at the next Gene- ral Election will result in the unseating of several Liberal members who now repre- sent Northern borough constituencies. This calculation is, of course, based on the assump- tion that those who vote for the labour candidates will he drawn almost. entirely from the Liberal ranks. The Sheffield contest tends to discredit this assumption. It would now seem that about one-third—or one voter in every three—of those who supported the Independent Labour candidate have been drawn from amongst that "Tory Democracy " which has been so assiduously cul- tivated during the last few years. Evidently the • workingmen who have been beguiled by the , blandishments of the free lances—or, shall we say, the free promisers ?—of Conservatism are beginning to discover that Tory Democracy is a sham. There was a certain plausibility about the methods of Lord RANDOLPH CHURCHILL when he was an authority in the Conservative party, but no one can pretend that Lord SALISBURY is much concerned a bout the welfare of anybody except aristocrats and plutocrats. All the efforts of Tory politicians in Parliament have lately bean directed towards shielding wealthy landlords and the moneyed classes generally from a fair share of taxation, with the intention, of course, of placing heavier burdens upon the backs of those who already are uuduly weighted. Perhaps this has led to a good deal of di'aillusionment in many quarters. At all events there are two in ferences that may be fairly drawn from the Atter- cliffe election. One is that the Toryism which is typified in the Marquis of SALISBURY and the Duke of DEvoNsHusa is repellent to the working; classes. The second is that the running of Inde- pendent Labour candidates will not be se detri- mental to the Liberal party as some Conservatives have foncil imagined.
LOCAL NEWS.
TRFAT TO 520 POOR SCHOOL CHILDREN AT RUNCORN.

'ffift Scrutiny Committee met at the Town Hall, Run- corn on Wednesday-evening for the purpose of selecting the names of those children sufficiently poor to be en- titled to tickets of the annual treat which takes place on the 25th inst. The school visitors, Messrs. T. Bowyer and Howard, submitted a list of between 500 and 600 names of poor s;lhool children, out of which tho Com- mittee selected 520. The place chosen for the treat is Mersey View, Overton Hills, Frodsham, and it is to be hoped that the day will be a fine one in order that the youngsters may enjoy themselves thoroughly. The tickets are being distributed by the teachers, at the var- ious schools prior to the midsummer holidays.

STREET BETTING AT WIDNES. At Widnes on Thursday, two men named David Andrews and Robert Roach pleaded guilty to obstructing the footpath by taking bets on the 3rd inst. It was stated that a crowd of a dozen people was round Andrews making b,lts. Superintendent Keighley asked the bench to inflict the highest penalty. It was very difficult for the police to catch these met', as thuy had scouts out. It was becoming a great nuisance at dinner- time, when lads and women and men congregated round these men making bets.—The Chairman said they would not inflict the full penalty on that occasion, but this street betting must be stopped, as it was becoming a great nuisance in the town. A fine of 20s. and costs was imposed in each case, with the alternative of fourteen days imprisonment.

div.head: RUNCORN RATEPAYERS AND THE COUNTY RATE BASIS.
div.p: RUNCORN RATEPAYERS AND THE COUNTY RATE BASIS.

A meeting of ratepayers took place on Thursday -eV'en- ing in the Bethesda Lecture Hall, Runcorn, Mr. W. Handley in the chair, for the purpose of considering the proposed County Rate Basis as prepared by the Com- mittee. Figures were submitted which showed that the basis upon which Runcorn has been paying was £53280, and the amount of the basis now proposed was £65006, making an increase of £11,726. The nett poor rate aSsessment in December 1893 was £58,669. After some discussion it was decided on the proposition of Mr. D. Bisbrown seconded by Mr. William Bell" that Messrs. E. unison and W. Handley be appointed a deputation to wait upon the Assessment Committee with a view to getting the new basis reduced to the poor rate aisessment, or an explanation obtained as to how the County Council arrived at such basis." The meeting closed with a vote of thanks to the Chairman.

A VIOLENT SOLDIER AT WIDNES. On Tbursday,at the Widnes Petty Sessions,before Mr. F. A. Stapleton-Bretherton and Councillor W. W. (Jos- sage, James Smith, of the North Lincashire Regiment, stationed at Preston,was charged on remand with creat- ing a breach of the peace in Pear-st. on Monday night, and also with assaulting Inspector Strickland and Police- sergeant Fretwell. The last-named officer was called to a disturbance at the fouse of the prisoner's parents. When he knocked at the door prisoner rushed out of the house, and struck the sergeant in the mouth with his clenched list. The inspector met Fretwell taking the prisoner to the Police Station, and Smith broke away from the officer and struck the inspector in the mouth. Superintendent Keighley said the prisoner was an ab- sentee from his regiment without leave. He had three previous omivictions recorded against him. The first charge was withdrawn, and for the assaults on the police the prisoner was committed to gaol for twenty- eight days with hard labour, without the option of a fiiae. RUNCORN BROKERS AND TIIE GRAVING DOCK QUESTION.

The brokers and traders of Runcorn are drawing up a petition to the Improvement Commissioners in reference to the proposed provision of a graving dock at Runcorn by the Manchester Ship Canal Company. The petition- ers desire that the wh(4le amount shall not 13(1 spent in providing a graving dock, but wish that better accom- modation should be provided with a portion, in order that trade might be attracted to the town. They state that the present means have been utilized and that the town is losing that trade which it would certainly enjoy if there was more extensive accommoda- tion for the vessels. Several timber ships which had been intended for Runcorn had either .stopped at Liverpool or gone forward to Man- chester when their shippers heard that not sufficient ac- commodation was available at Runcorn. The brokers and traders consider that this question is of vital import- ance to Runcorn, and prophesy increased trade if the facilities for accommodating vessels are augmented.

THE PLANS FOR THE WINWICK LUNATIC ASYLUM.

The Plans Committee of the Lancashire As3-lums Board met on Wednesday to consider which plan should be accepted for the erection of the new Win- wick Asylum. After much consideration it was unanimously resolved_ .to report to the Board at a special meeting to be called that the committee con- sidered that the plan of Alessrs.FLCrisp and Oakley, of Bristol, should be the one approved of,subject no doubt to some minor alterations which in the case of any plan would have to be made. The first esti- mate for the plan now approved was the highest of the three that were awarded premiums. On going, however, into the details and placing the amounts of each on a common basis, it was found that only some two or three thousand pounds was the sum in difference. This simplified the labours of the com- mittee, and left the plan regarding the arrange- ments of the buildings for ultimate decision, when .the committee approved, all of them being of one mind in the matter. The cost of the new asylum will be about £245,000.

At the termination of the public business of the Warrington Board of Guardians on Wednesday, the Board resolved themselves into a committee to con- sider the proposed orders of the Joint Committee of the Lancashire and Cheshire County Councils with reference to the separation of the Cheshire town- ships from the Warrington Union. and their addi- tion to the Runcorn Union. The Clerk having read a lengthy statement thereon, and the matter hav- ing been fully discussed, it was resolved that such decision be appealed against, and the Clerk was also empowered to take any other steps he might, deem necessary to that effect. It having been men- tioned that the Rev. G. F. Roberts, Mr. Ileaton,and the clerk to the Rural 'Sanitary Authority would be in Londoti attending the Sanitary Congress at the end of-the present month, and the Clerk to the Guardians having also business in London about the ARM° time, it was decided that these gentle,men should wait upon the Local government Board and discuss the matter with them. It came to the knowledge of the sanitary authorities in Runcorn on Monday that a man named Barker, aged 41 years, and apparently a boatman, was suffering from smallpox. He was at once reni.ved to the Runcorn In- fectious Diseases Hospital and every possible effort was put f@rth by the authorities to prevent the sprad of the malignant disease. From inquiries which have been made it app•::ars that the man had been recently engaged on canal boats in the vicinity of Manchester and had walked from Stretford to Runcorn on Monday. On Thursday evening he was reported to be improving.

div.head: RUICCOLIN ASSOCIATION FOOTBALL CLUB.
div.p: RUICCOLIN ASSOCIATION FOOTBALL CLUB.

A general meeting of the members of .the above club was held on Monday evening last, Mr. H. McLeod pre- siding. The chief item on the agenda was the consider- ation of the advisability of joining an association. The advantages to be derived through becoming affiliated with an association were pointed out and the matter fully discnssed. Finally it was resolved unanimously to join the Warrington and District Association. It was ,tated that the old field had been re-engaged and that a successful season was anticipated. A vote ot thank; to the chairman terminated the meeting.. STARVATION CASE AT *i'VIDNE.3. On Thursday at the Widnes Petty Sessions, before Mr. F. A. Stepleton-Bretherton and Councillor W. W. Gossage, Samuel Mercer, labourer, and his wife Ann Mercer, were summoned ky the National Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Children for haying wilfully neglected their child, a girl ten years of age, in such a manner as to cause her necessary pain and suffering. Mr. Buckton, of Warrington represented the scciety. It appears that the child is one of five Oildren. The male detendant earned about 19s. per week, but kept no re- gular home. The child only weighed 371bs instead of about 501bs. The male defendant was sentenced to three months with hard labour, and the woman for one month with hard labour. A MERSEY DROWNING MYSTERY.

On Tuesday morning at the Hunt's Cross Hotel, Mr. S. Brighouse, county coroner, held an inquest on the body of a man unknown which was found on the shore of the Mersey at Speke on Saturday evening. Toe body was that of a man from twenty-six to thirty years of age, 51t. 81n., long dark brown hair, slight moustache (dark), and no whiskers. It was supposed the man Wai drowned while bathing. The jury brought in a verdict. of" Found drowned," and suggested that some pro- vision should be made for dead bodies in the townsnip. this being the second found drowned recently.—The Coroner said he believed it was the duty of the overseer to look after bodies cast up by the tide. div.p: BATHING FATALITY AT WIDNES.

On Friding morning, Mr. F. A. Jones, deputy county coroner, held an inquest a the Police Station, touching the death of a youth named Henry Morley, aged 16, of 12 Cholmondelepstreet, Widnes. The deceased left home about six o'clock on 'Thursday the sth inst. saying that IC wal going to play crick, t. It appears, howc.ver, that I.e went to West Hank Dock for a bathe in company ia h William Cm:, aged 18, of 38 Oakland-street. Cox had got out of the water and was dressing when he noticed the deceased strop:ling in the water. He at once dive- ted hitrs-11 of his clothing and swam to the aid of his companion and managed to grab hold of one of his fingers but could not stick to him and he sank. Grap- pling irons were used and eventually the body was re- covered. Alter hearing the evidence the jury returned a verdict of " Accidental dclith " and recommended that Cox's plucky attempt to save the deceased's life he brought before the notice of the Royal flutrianeSociety. div.head: ACCIDENT TO A PASSENGER STEAMER AT RUNCORN.
div.p: ACCIDENT TO A PASSENGER STEAMER AT RUNCORN.

_ On Thursday afternoon at about two o'clock, as the steam ship "Manx Fairy was approaching Runcorn Bridge on her way to Manchester one of her steam pipes burst and further progress was prevented. She had a fair number of passengers on board at the time of the occurrence many of whom were bent on important business to Cottonopollis. The steamer was laid up at the Old Quay yard to undergo repairs which were not completed until three hours had elapsed. The passengers, when they learnt the nature of the accident, and the time which would be occupied in repairing the pipe, decided to resume their jouiney on board the " Prince George," another passenger steamer which was on its way to Manchester. The "Manx Fairy." afterwards continued her course up the canal to Manchester, without further mishap.

A DETERMINED SUICIDE AT SANKEY BRIDGES.

A suicide of a very determined character, took place at Sankey Bridges, between two and three o'clock on Saturday morning. A man was seen ou the river bank near Monks,Hall, and Co.'s works,to divest himself.of his coat and vest and then jump into the river. A strong tide was coming up the river at the time, and the man was carried towards Warrington. A man named William Ede,who was employed as a watchman on the dredgers at Bank Quay,saw the man, and procured a boat and pushed off to his assistance,but was unable to save him. The ' river was dragged on Saturday morning with grap- pling irons, but the body was not recovered. On the coat pockets of the man being searched,a letter addressed to William Moran, 36, Howard-street, Sankey Bridges, was found in them. The tenants of that house were at once communicated with,and they identified the clothing as that of Wm. Moran, who was 29 years of age. The body was recovered on Tuesday, a little higher up the river than where the deceased was seen to jump in. The inquest was held by Mr. S. Brighouse on Thurs- day morning, at the Black Horse Inn, Sankey Bridges. William Moran, the father of the deceased said that his son resided with him at 36 Howard-st. He was a sofa spring and sieve maker by trade, but had been out of wiork since Christmas, during which time, witness had kept him. The last time witness saw his son alive was on Tuesday, the 3rd inst. On Saturday morning lie was returning from his work, and heard that someone had jumped into the river, and meeting the policeman with. the clothes in his possession, he at once identified them as belonging to his son. Witness did not know of any reason why his son had done away with himself, but he had had very bad rest at night. He was drinking on the morning when witness last saw him.—Richard Moran said that he was brother of deceased. From Tuesday the 3rd inst. to Thursday they had been drinking to- gether, and on Thursday they had spent all their money. During Tuesday and Wednesday nights they had slept it Arpley meadows and Dallam Forge. They parted in Tanner's-lane on Thursday, and witness never saw deceased again alive. He was sober at that time.—Win. Ede, waterman, 36 Regent at., Runcorn, said that he. was in the employ of the Ship Canal Company. Between two and three o'clock on Saturday morning he saw. the deceased jump into the river. Witness at once got a boat to go to his assistance, but the deceased sank,before the boat reached him. It was just breaking day when the man jumped into the river. The deceased made a run across the bank before he jumped into the river. He never called for help. Witness saw the body pulled-out on Tuesday, and it was taken to the residence of de- ceased's lather.—The jury after about five minutes' consultation, returned a verdict of "Suicide whilst temporarily insane."

div.head: COMPETITORS AT TIIE CRYSTAL PALACE.
div.p: COMPETITORS AT TIIE CRYSTAL PALACE.

Our local tonic sol-faists will on Saturday parti- cipate in the great choral festival of the Tonic Sol- Fa Association, at the Crystal Palace, London. The choristers will leave Runcorn by train this (Friday) evening, for London, and will be accompanied by Mr. John Ho!ford, their conductor. In the morning at eleven o'clock they will take part in 5 glee party compe- tition, whilst in the afternoon, at about four o'clock, the" will perform the new sacred cantata speciilly com- posed for the occasion by Mr. Henry Coward, Mus. Bee. OxQn., and entitled "The King's Error." They will also engage in a miscellaneous selection of music. The choir gave an open rehearsal in the Ellesmere. Schoolroom, Runcorn, on Tuesday evening of the music to be sung by them in the glee party com- petition. This consists of Henry Smart's " The Shepherd's Lament," which is the test piece for all competitive choirs. In addition they will perform a piece of their own selection, and Runcorn has chosen Dr. Hile's " Hushed in Detth." This they sang twice on Tuesday night in order that the audience might have an idea of the _work. Thay also gave a glee from Oberon, " In Fairyland," and Sir Henry Bishop's" Fisherman's good-night." Songs were contributed by Mrs. Temper- lev. Miss K. Edwards, Messrs. Worrall, Leathwood, and Shingler, and the qua' tette " Ora Pro Nobis" by Mesdaines Temperley, and Stubbs, and Messrs. Worrall and Pendlebury. Mr. S. Coventry, who occupied the position of chairman spoke in terms of praise af the performances, and congratulated the choir upon their achievement. Ile expressed an earnest hope that they would be successful in bringing back the. first prize. Mr. John •Holfard acted as conductor in his usual effi- cient manner, and Mr. Wm. Cooke ably presided at the piano. It may he mentioned tint the composer, Mr. Henry Coward attended the rehearsal, and expressed himself as more than pleased with the manner in which the choir had performed the cantata, and the intelligent grasp they had obtained of it. • _

D ETERM IN ED ACTION. On Thursday- evening a meeting of ratepayers was held in the National Saools, Weston, for the purpose of considering the proposed standard of the county rate, and also what action to take in reference to the insufficient water supply from the Run- corn Improvement Commissioners to the township of Weston. Mr. E. Aaron, overseer, was voted to the chair, and the attendance included Messrs. James Col- lier, a,sistant'overseer ' • J. Vose, 0. D. Lloyd, T. Ford, Reilly, Leach, Nesbitt, D. Kirkham, Sze. Mr. Collier being called upon by the Chairman,stated that the preeent county rate basis, at fixed five years ago, was £12,368, but that now proposed by the Assess- ment Committee of the Cheshire County Council was £13,157,nr an increase of £791 on the rateable value for the next five years. The Chairman thought the increase was very exces- sive, especially when the present state cf Weston was taken intoconsiderath n. 'The township was practically in a position of bankruptcy and it was beyond all reason that the county authorities should increase the rite to such an enormous amount. He suggested that they should write to the Aesessment Committee of the Rue- corn Union and request them to direct the Clerk to lodge an ebjeetion to the high increase. - In answer to several retepayers, Mr. Collier said the steps taken five years ago when the county rate was increased resulted in their asking the Assessment Com- mittee of the Ruecorn Union to appeal against the incre:ve at that time. He explained that in reality the present increase was only about 2400, and in view of the rumours that the seapworks were to be extended shortly, as well as other projected developments, he did not think it advisable to appeal against the increase. The Chairman thought that it was not wise to depend too much simply upon hearsay. Nothing was known, as a matter of fact, what improvements, if any, werc being projected concerning the works. Eventually it was proposed by Mr. Voys, seeonded by Mr. Ford, and carried that the assistant overseer write to the Assessment Committee of the Runcorn Union and ask them to instruct Mr. Ashton, their clerk, to object to , the increase. -

div.head: TUE INSUFFICIENT WATER SUPPLY.
div.p: TUE INSUFFICIENT WATER SUPPLY.

The Chairman said they now came ti the vexed cities- tion of th, inadequate supply of water to the township by the Runcorn Improvement Commissioners. There were many there that twening who knew what difficulties they in Kiestow often laboured under to procure water for domestic purposes. He himself had several times called upon the secretary of the Commisioners and bid the complaint before him. He had likewise written many times but all to no use. The answer always was that the Commissioners had done all they could, and that it was impossible for them to do more Mr. \rose had also moved in the matter but their joint efforts had not met with success. People were paying rates for water which they had never tIAKI. He had gone into his own sellar for water at eleven o'clock at night. and could not get any. This was when none could be gut the room above. They had been several days without a drop of water in the house. _ _

-.- Many of the ratepayers present re-echoed the ramarks of Mr. Aaron, one of them saying that he had been in his house from siN o'clock in the onorning to eleven at night and could not get water. Another said that he had had to wait on many occasions fully hill-an-hour before a bucket was filled with water from his tap so poor was the supply or the pressure. The Chairman remarked that some time ago Mr. J. Farrington, nuisance inspector to the Runcorn Rural Sanitary Authority, was crdered to investigate the sup- posed inadequate supply 'of water. lie did SO with the result that lie found 100 houses with an insufficient sup- ply. He wrote to the Commissioners upon the matter, but they had not taken any notice of it. In the first place it was proposed that legal advice should be sought with a view to compelling the Runcorn I Commissioners to provide a proper supply, but an amendment was moved that a deputation be sent to the Commissioners to lay the matter tefore them for the last time. If nothing was done then a solicitor should be engaged. M. Vose subsequently amended his original proposition so as to intriduce the amendment giving toe overseers the power to pot the matter in the hands of a RoliCitOr should the deputation not he satisfi,td. This on being put to the meeting was unanimously carried, and the following gentlemen el(rted as a deputation : Messrs. E. Aaron, John Vose, D. Kirthaln, Nesbitt, and James Collier assistant overseer.
lho proceedings terminated with a vote of thank; to the Chairman.

div.p: MESSRS. FAIRCLOUGH AND THE SHIP
CANAL.

On Saturday, a meeting of the Corporation, and manufacturers of Warrington was held at the offices of Messrs. Greenall and Buckton, to further consider the terms of settlement between Messrs. Fairelough. and the Ship Canal Co. The Corporation were recommended not to approve of the terms, and as a result of the meting, the Town Clerk sent an. official notice to the Ship Canal Co. to the effect that the Corporation declined to sanction the proposed agreement.

On Tuesday afternoon, Mr. Warmington, Q.C., applied to Mr. Justice Kekewich to restore to the paper the action of Fairclough v. the Manchester Ship Canal Co., as the parties had not come to terms. His Lordship said that he could not then 'definitely fix a day, owing to the present state of his list- In the meantime the law agents of the two nartiee still continue their negotia:ions toward a settlement. The Ship Canal Co. have not yet completd the dredving of the river,and have there- fore, by. the Act of Parliament, been under a penalty of £5O per day since July Ist.
INSTANTANEOUS DEATH OF A RAILWAY SERVANT.

ATTEMPTED LEAP FROM A MOVING TRAIN An accident winch unfortunately was attended with a fatal result occurred to a young man named Griffiths Jones, of Handbridge, Chester, on Monday morning at Helsby railway station. It appears that Jones, nho was a fireman on the Great WeAtern Railway, and a native of Shrewsbury, was told off to, relieve another servant and to join the train at Helsbv. Accordingly he entered the 11.33 train from Chester tO Liverpool which up to the end of June had stopped at Helsby, but after thkt date it had been announced that the train would not stop. Not until nearing Helsbv station did Jones become aware of this alteration and then he appeared to have opened the door of his com- partment with the intention of leaping on to the plat- form. Owing to relaying operations the train slackened its speed to the rate of from twelve to fifteen miles an hour. By some means the foot ,of the unfortunate man became entangled with the footboard, and when the train arrived at the station he fell forward and was dragged by the train along the top of the platform and afterwards on to the metals. The body presented a fearful spectacle, some of the limbs being tern away and the head smashed. The remains were afterwards con- veyed to the Railway Inn, where on Tuesday after- noon Mr. Churton held an inquest. After hearing the evidence, the jury returned a verdict of "Accidental death." .

div.head: SONS OF TEMPERANCE.
div.p: SONS OF TEMPERANCE.
-PUBLIC MEETING AT EARLESTOWN.

Under the auspices.of the Britain's Need divis.ion of the :ions of Temperance, nn open air meeting was. held on the Market Place, Earlestown, on Wednes- day evening. There was a very fair audience. Bro.. W. 11. Adams, of Latchford, presided, and he was accompanied on the impromptu platform by Bro. W. liallsworth (Salford), W. Pearson, U.S., and Pickett.

Bro. Pearson briefly ietroduced the chairman, who said the temperance cause waa by no means new to him.. It was twenty-two years since he ha 0 joined the Sons of Temperance, and some years ago he had taken an active interest in the work of temperance in Earlestown, but. he had been called away, and although he did not now actively identify himself with the Earlestown branch,. still he had the cause at heart. (Hear, hear.) Mr. O. Pickett, said he had been asked to speak on the juvenile branch of the order. The order which they represented that night had a branch for children, and would take children from five years of age at a contriba- ' don of lid. per week, and bring them up as total abstainers, aud it death should happen in six months, their panels woulA receive £3 103., in twelve months. £6. and in three years £B. At the age of 16 they trans- ferred them into the adult societv, and he was sure there was no insurance society gave the same benefits tor the same 'contributions. They had now got 100 members, and the cause was a good and safe one. He had belonged to it 23 years, and he had received great benefits from it. He had received more out of it for less money than he had out of any society to which he paid heavier cou- tributions. They would bring the children up to tem-. perance, so that when they grew older they cyanid become useful citizens eno take part in the government of the town. (Hear, hear.) Mr. W: Ilalisworth said they were proposing in the House of Commons that they should have pure beer,and if they had that they would have better health. rhe- temperance patty had told them before that they had not had pure beer, and they had told them that as teeto- tallers they lived longer and haii less sickness than men who attended public-houses. Take the annual report of the Oidfellows, the Foresters, Druids and Shepherds,. all of which were not organisations composed of men who were drunkards, but of thrifty working men, who. -joined nefore the Sens of Temperance were ore,fanised. or the Rechabit.es were brought into existence. Take- the annual report of the Sons of Temperance, and com- pare it with any of the Societies he had named, and they would .find that whereas those Societies buried 14 or 15. men in the 1,000 the Sons of Temperance buried 7 or 8 per 1,000, and where they paid 14 days sick money per , man, the latter Society only IMO 6 or 7.1 days per member. Looking at it from a religious point, he said there was no greater enemy to the Sunday schools than. the public-house of the present day. Public-hon.:ea would only exist, inasmuch as the people were prepared to fold their arms. 7 here was no better organisation for- keeping their lads and lasses to the Sunday school, than getting them identified with the S.ins of Temperance. They mere fighting the liquor traffic, and were giving them no quarter. He asked them fay; only to sign the , pledge, to join the Sons of Temperanee, but to take hart in the rovvrntn,mt of the country, of which they foraied, apa t. Applause.) After a vote of thanks to the speakers the gatluTing.- dispersed.

There was no furniture, and only a kinarter of a pyund of bread in the house. D.S. Monaghan and Sergeant Chsintler who had also visited the house corroborated the inspector's statement. fhe husband on being questinnod sdd that when he was working full time he earned 255. a week, and had never neglected his children in his life. The case was adjourned for one month in or&r that the defendant's conduct might be watched.

AGGRAVATED ASSAULT ON A WiFE.—Win.Fincli,husband of Charlo`te Amn Finch, Pierpoint-3t.,was charged with having on the 27th June, beaten and assaulted his wife. Mr. Davies represented the complainant and Mr. Knowles solicitor, Widnes, appeared for the defence. Mr. Davies stated that the complainant was a greenf!rocer, and was the wife of the defendant, who was a traveller for his father. At 12.30 on the morning of the date named,the defendant came home drunk. Atter having his supper the complainant asked him for his wages, telling him that he had only given her 9s. in a month. The com- plainant had four children, and this was all the defend- ant had given her for their maintenance. On the de- fendant only offering her Bs. she complained to him about it. He thereupon struck her a violent blow under the left breast. This stiggered her a little, but she managed to get the poker. This the defendant took off her.anci struck her with it across the back, and left her. lyinc, on the floor. He had not been to the house since Charlotte Ann Finch corroborated Mr. Davies's state- ment, and said she was confined to the house several days through the injuries she received. The defendant was nearly always drunk. In cross-examination she denied that he had ever commenced to attend the meet- ings of the Wycliffe P.S.A. Society, she would have been glad if he had done so. Martha Edwards and Thomas Wilcock gave evidence as to seeing the defendant strike the complainant. Mr. Knowles, for the defence, in a lengthy hut humourous address to the Bench, contended that it was only a common assault, and that it was six of one and half-a-dozen of the other. The Chairman said the Bench were agreed that an aggravated assault had been committed, and imposed a fine of 20s. and costs. They granted a separation ordn,and ordered the defend- ant to pay 12s. per week towards his wife's mainten- ance. _ .

div.head: COAL TRADE
div.p: THE COAL TRADE

Mr. T. Ashton on Monday sent out to the various dis- tricts the term; of settlement which were unanimously agreed to at a joint meeting of the representatives of bath the waalowners and miners federations. The terms are these :-1. That the present rate of wages be re- duced, as from the Ist Atwust, 1894, bY takintc off the last two advances of 5 per cent each, and that the wags remain at that rate until toe let January,lB96. 2. That for a period of two years from the Ist August, 1894. the rate of wages shall not be below 30 por cent above the rate of waaes of 1838, nor more than 45 per cent above the rate of wa‘res of 1888. 3. 'That from the Ist Janu- ary, 1896, to the Ist Augli-t, 1896, the rate of wages shall be determined by the Conciliation Board within the above-named limits. 4: That the Conciliation Board shall be continued for this purpose for two years from Ist August, 1894. It is believed that sr, fAr as the men are concerned these terms will be accepted.

The delegates felt that, in view or the varied expressions of opinion on the part both of miaers and coalowners, the suhi.ct should first he dis- cussed by the men at their varied pithead and district meetin,s. With regard te, the strike of Scotch miners, the action of the Executive in ordering a levy of is. per member per week was approved.

div.p: Sir Gilbert has retired from public notice almost alto- gether. His health was not of the best, and he went to reside with his son at Tarporley, where his condition changed for the worse, and he gradually sank, and died on Tuesday, as above stated. Notwithstanding his long Parliamentary career, Sir Gilbert has been very unobtrusive, and he took no part whatever in the dis- cussions in the House of Commons. "Essence of Parliament," by "Toby "in "Punch," is a good criter- ion of the amoant of publicity a member of Parliament obtains, and it might be mentioned that the only skit about Sir Gilbert was about five years ago, when some new rules with regard to the taking of divisions had come into vogue in the House of Commons, and Sir Gilbert was represented as having lost his way in the division lobby, and having found himself in the cellars below the House. A sketch was also made showing him groping his way about. , Sir Gilbert is, as is well-known, a very successful brewer, his ales being known throughout the kingdom, and it is in this trade that he has acquired the greater part of his large fortune. He has been a very generous benefactor to the Church, and during the late disastrous coal dispute, he gave a large donation each week to the distress fund esta,blishel at Warrington. The deceased baronet was a prominent freemason, and one of the lodges has been named after him.

div.head: NEW BARONET.
div.p: THE NEW BARONET.

The new Baronet, Sir Gilbert Greenall, was born on the 30;.h of March, 1867 and is therefore in his 28± year. For some years past he has taken a strong interest in all matters pertaining to agriculture, but more particularly in the breeding of horses and cattle. As is well-known, he has this year taken nearly everything before him at the Royal and other shows, and the deep interest he has taken all along in the improvement of farm stock can- not hut have proved immensely b .nefieial to the large number of tenants on the Greenall estates. THE NEW ESTATE DUTY.

It is stated in a House of Commons paper explanatory of the proposal of the Chancellor of the Exchequer with respect to the new Estate Duty that" the duty will be payable upon the capital value of all property which passes on the death of a person dying after the 31st May, 1894." The amount of duty payable on an es,we valued at. £lOO,OOO to'£lso,ooo be £6,000 to £9,000 or 6 per cent ; £250,000 to £500,000 £17.500 to £35,000, or 7 per cent.; £500,000 to £1,000,000 £37,500 to £75_000, or 71 per cent; £1,000,000 and upwards £BO,OOO and upwards or 8 per cent. div.head: GUARDIANS.
div.p: GUARDIANS.

At the close of the usual business of the Warrington Board of Guardians, Mr. William Houghton (the chair- man) referring to the death of Sir Gilbert Greenall, said that a well known figure in Warrington and the County had passed away. The event had not been unexpected, and it was felt that it must come in a short time. At the same time, an important body like the Board of Guardians,he thought,should notice such an occurrence, and do something in the way of smding a vote of condo- Lilice to Lady Greenall, expressing their sorrow at the sad event. Many of the Guardians, knew more than he did about Sir Gilbert, and they would perhaps say some- thing themselves. He begged to vote that a vote of con- dolence be passed to L.idy Greenall and her family,and a copy of the resolution be sent to Lady Greenall.—Mr. R. Heaton seconded the motion. He said that he felt sure everyone knew of the good work Sir Gilbert had done while living,and every member of the Board would feel regret at his death. He had lived to a ripe old age, and his death therefore was not unexpected.—The motion was carried unanirnously.

NEWTON'S REPRESENTATIVE.

Sir,—lt appears that at the last Commissioners meeting; the Chairman once more desired to make Mr. Smith into a Newton representative, or rather to say he was. The Committee of Newton ratepayers, who have lately been trying to do something tor Newton, desire once more to repudiate the suggestion that they have any representa- tive but Colonel McCorquodale. The Chairman proposed Mr. Smith's election as Commissioner and Mr. Thompson seconded the proposition. the Newton electors were never asked to express any opinion on the matter. As I write I am informed that the Chairman, Mr. Ormand, and Mr. Smith have beers to London to endeavour to get the head Post Office removed to Earlestown from New- ton, I do not think this looks like the action of a "Newton representative." The old proverb says, " A man is known by the company he keeps," this seems to be still true.—Yours faithfully,
ROBERT STUART.
Laurel Bank, Newton-le-Willows.
THE PREVENTION OF CRUELTY TO CHILDREN.

Sir,—While still with the remembrance of Hospital Sunday and its magnificent collections fresh in our minds, it falls to me as the Chairman of the Central Committee of this Society to make yet another appeal to the benevolent public in the hope that a sufficient sum may be raised to pay off the debt that has accumulated during the last year, and also to raise a reserve fund so that the financial position of the Scciety may be placed upon a thoroughly sound footing. We have to tear in mind that during the ten years this Society has existed, its area, and necessarily its work, with the large expenses accruing to it, have increased by leaps and bounds—more particu- larly so during the last year, and, at the same time, its finances have suffered with many other philanthropic works from the general depression Though the subscriptions and dcnations last year amounted to £40,000, this did not come up to the es-. timated increase of income in proportion to the number of cases inquired into, and leaves the Society with a debt of £6,000. Hitheito the Society has gone upon the humane principle of taking up every wo.se brought under its notice; but unless tnis &lot is wiped off and provi- sion can be made for the gradual formation of the re- serve fund, the machinery, now in good working order, must be stopped, and the cry of the suffering, cruelly- treated children will go up to Heaven unanswered. The generous public, who have supported the Society in the past, and who, I have every belief, will come to our assistance in our present strait, may rest assured that the Committee, with the able and hearty concur- rence of the Hon. Director (the Rev. Benjamin. Waugh) will endeavour to administer the affair-4 of the Society with every possible economy; but it can- not be denied that it is a costly work, and when we see the large results that have been obtained, the useful legislation for children carried through Parlia- ment, and that the children who have been succoured during the ten years of the existence of the Society number 109,000 (see report far 1894, " Justice to Children," page 9), we can only marvel at the facts be- fore us, at the success achieved. And knowing the deep interest excited in the breasts of all humane people for these little sufferers from no fault of their own, to whom the sacred name of " home" conveys only misery, we, the committee, feel that we cannot appeal in vain. Contributions may be sent, marked " Special Fund," to Coutts and Co„ Strand, London, W.C.. ; or to Rev. Benjamin Waugh, 7, Harpur-street, London, WC.—I am, yours, &c.,
ANCASTEIZ, Chairman.
NEWTON POSTAL ARRANGEMENTS &c.

Sir,—l observe frem the report in last issue of your paper that the Chairman of Commissioners stated Mr. Smith was a representative of Newton, but what are the facts in connection with this : Mr. Gillespie, one of the Newton representatives was so thoroughly disgusted generally with the management of town affairs that at the beginning of the year he resigned his seat on the Board Mr. Smith was selected to take his plane but by whom? Certainly not by the Newton people. Tlze New- ton people were not consulted,or referred to in any way. Newton has a Representative Comi,nittee which has made the Commissioners feel their position. Yet this Com- mittee was not consulted. Your readers lam sure, will say this is all quite true and they will say further, it is equally true that Mr. Smith was selected, by Mr. Em- mett and his Earlestown friends solely. This being so the Chairman of Commissioners must have a very poor estimation of Newton intelligence when he endeavours to palm Mr. Smith on them as cue of their representa- tives. Yet, when I remember this is not the first time Mr. Emmett has done a similar thing. When the New- ton ratepayers deputation waited on the Conimissioner3 at last back end re the wards question. Mr. Emmett made a determined effort to thurst Mr. E. T. Evans on it as a Newton representative but this was repudiated all round; and it would now appear that Mr. Emmett tacitly admits he was then wrong, when he has not brought Mr. Evans to the front, in a similar manner at the present time. Mr. Smith was an active member of the Commissioners deputation which waited on Mr. Rich re-postal arrangements some weeks ago and it would seem that he did such good service for Earles- town at Liverpool then,that I am informed Mr. Emmett and Mr. Ormand took him wjth them on the London deputation last week, to the post office officials there, on the some question. Fellow ratepayers for Newton will you remember this next November ? Mr. Emmett, the Chairman of the Commissioners, has had the principal hand in erecting a building at a cost of £lO,OOO instead of £5,000 as agreed, in a place en- tirely inconvenient to the town as a whole, and it now seems that he is going in for a new Pest Office for the con- venience of his own part of the town, and ignoring the other part. Will the people allow this to be done by a mbribund Board which does not represent them, and which now holds its positions on sufferance for a few months only,or will they insist that the question should stand over until a new Board is appointed ? I consider the gentlemen of the Newton deputation put their views before Mr. Rich in an honest and manly way. They took a reporter with them on the. distinct understanding that he would give an unbiassed report. They went at their own expense, and they deserve our best thanks, what- ever may he the result.—Yours respectfully, Newton,July 12th, 194.
A. NEWTON RATEPAYEII.

PAROCHIAL COMMITTEE.-At the fortnightly meeting, of the Runcorn Sanitary Authority, Mr. John Mclntyre presiding, on Tuesday afternoon, the minutes of the last meeting of the Halton Parochial Committee on the 7th inst., were submitted for confirmation. The minutes stated that a letter was read from the Local Govern- ment Board, referring to the eollution of Haiton Brook, and inquiring what had since been done in the matter, It was resolved that the Clerk 'reply referring to his letter of the 21st February, and forward it copy of Dr. Adams' report submitted to the Authority previous to the agreement with Sir Richard Brooke being entered into. A communication was read from Mr.C.L. Evan, ,agent to Sir R. M. Brooke, saying he had not promised to connect the boys' school with the Runcorn Water Works. He asked Mr. Farrington to meet him and give 'him his opinion as t 6, the best and most economical way of bringing the Runcorn water to the schools,and unless another scheme which he had in mind could be carried ,out, no doubt such would be done. The water in Keck- wick Brook was as bad on the previous day as it ever had been, polluted by the tannery at Preston Brook. i'le asked to be informed when the inspector would visit Halton Gate and other farms to take samples of the water as he desired to meet him there.—Mr. Farrington reported that be had taken one sample and intended to take the other en Monday, and it was ordered that the .Clerk reply to that effect.—The minute 3 were approved by the Authority.
UNSOUN'D MRAT.

On Tuesday, Mest:ln-spect.)r Stoirthwaite seized, at the St. Helens Corvration slaughtpr-house, the C41T:160 of a cow which had been dresse..l for sale, but vvls in a deceased condition. Dr. Robertson, medical offic:er for St. Helens, certified that the mat was totally unfit for human food, and in the afternoon a magistrates' order for its destruction was made.
IOTtS ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS. CRICKET.

Warrington met the Cheetham Hill Club on Saturday at Arpley, and a defeat for the home team was again the result. It was the first meeting of the two clubs this season, and as the teams were considered to be of equal strength, a large number of spectators made their way to the Arpley enclosure to witness the match. An old face to followers of local cricket was soon recognised when the Cheetham Hill team entered the field, in the person of Mr. C. Lawton, for many years a local amateur cricketer, and who for some time did good service for the Warrington team. He has been away to New Zea- land playing with the wibow. On his return this year, the Cheetham Hill Club, for which club he had previ- ously been professional, again requisitioned his services.

Warrington were the first to have their innings, but run-getting by them, with the exception of Bates was " orf." The start was disastrous, the two initial bats- men, Messrs. R. Smith and %V. Mortimer, being dis- missed with only six runs scored. A slight improve- mient took place on Wordsworth and Bates becoming associated, but a separation soon came, the former player being stumped. The score stood at 21, for the loss of three wickets, and rain now began to fall which caused the players to hie themselves to the pavilion.

On the resumption of hostilities, Warrington's score improved immensely, one over of Lawton's, whose bowl- ing had proved too good for the first two batsmen,yield- ing eleven runs. Their success, however, was short-lived for at 43, Clarke was bowled, and by the time the score had reached 55, two other Warrington batsmen Bates and Callon, had been sent back to the pavilion. The most noticeable feature in the remainder of tho innings was the splendid bowling of Riley who took three wickets without a single run being scored from his bowl- ing. Warrington's score at the close of their innings was 85. Towards this Bates had contributed 26, and the only other batsmen who reached double figures were Griffin with 16 not out and Connor li.

The visitors opened their innings with H.S. Lang and Lawton, and these two scored rapidly. Before a sepa- ration had been effected they had compiled between them 55 runs. Lawton was the first tus be out, having scored 18. Only five more runs had been added when Lang fell a victim to a catch by Bates. Beeston and Riley. the two succeeding batsmen, however, set the re- suit of the match beyond doubt by passing the Warring- ton total by three before parting, when Bates had the credit of taking another wicket. At the call of time Cheetharn Hill had scored 105 for the less of six wickets. Bates was the best player for Warrington, coming off best man with the bat' and being most successful in bowling. To-day, the Warrington team are to meet Wigan,but as to the result I will refrain from prophesy- ing. The Warrington team seem to be following the had example set them by Lancashire County this season in the matter of winning matches.

The second team of Warrington, nearly,but not quite, managed to beat the Cheetham Hill second eleven on Saturday afternoon. The match was played at Cheet- ham Hill, but the Warrington men seem to have batted with quite as much freedom and confidence as if on their native heath. Their score of 203 runs was one to be proud of, but as after events proved, it would have been more to their advantage to have concluded their innings a little earlier. By not doing so they robbed themselves of an almost certain victory, for at the time of drawing stumps,the Cheetham Hill men had only put together 31 runs for the loss of five wickets. Toe match thus ended in a draw greatly in favour of the Warring- ton team. The chief contributors to the Warringtm score were Adamson 64, Woods 31, Duckwoith 27, and Hind (not out) 26.

The St. Mary's team had an easy time of it with the Halton Wesleyans on Saturday. for after closing their innings with the score at 110 for five wickets, they tumbled the Wesleyans out for 20. Among the batters Rigby and Jolly with 30 and 34 not out respectively, played an excellent game. Roddy was very deadly with the bat, taking seven wickets for as many runs. The last six wickets of the Halton Wwleyaus did not pro- duce a single run.

The Cheshire Lines Engineers had to submit to defeat for the second time this season, and that on their own ground. The conquerors were the Sankey Wire Mills, who had to thank Marshall and Hobson f6r their victory. Hobson took five of the Engineers' wickets for cnly ten runs, while Marshall, besides taking three wickets for five runs, scored ten runs, which was the highest score on his side. Harrison was the top scorer of the match with 13 not out, and in addition to this, he claimed six of the Wire Mills wickets. This victory is a very credit- able one for the Wire Mills, who have done very well thus far this season.

Buckley-st. met a selected team on Saturday, but the team sitlectd was not a v•-ry first class one, for whereas the selected ones only scored 15 between them, Buckley- street were not content with less than 70. Cairo-street Unity were two to one better than the Y.M.C.A. on Saturday, or to be more exact 45 to 22. The Y.M.C. A . are not going so strong as they did at the beginning of the season when they gained a few sewational victories.

div.head: CYCLING.
div.p: CYCLING.

On Saturday afternoon, twenty-five of the Warrington Cycling Club members set out for a run to Siddington. At High Legh, however, they were met with a most unwelcome thunderstorm, and this caused the wheelers to decide on some other spot than Siddington. Accrrd- ingly, they" trundled " along to Knutsford. Here they witnessed the Cheshire Lines sports, and had the satis- saction of seeing two of their members carry off priz•s. The event was the two miles bicycle handicap, and in this, J. Buxton won the second prize, and J. Whitham the third. For the run on Tuesday,the place of destina- tion was Newton, and after a most f niwable run in which thirty tlok part, they disported themselves on a bowling green and the lake until returning home time.

THE SUB-CAPTAIN of the Warrington Cycling Club.—Mr. TED PICICAvANCE, writes May 22, 1893. Dear Sir,—l have given your DRINKSTONE EMBROCA- TION an exhaustive trial and can safely recornr,end it as a good reliable article. A little of it rub e 0 into the muscles after a long ride gives a wonderfully soothing effect ; while for a Sprain I know of nothing better. lam confident that when its in7Tits are kno,n amongst Cyclists, and Athletes generally it w;11 command a great Sale. Yours truly, E. PICKAVANCe: To be obtsined only from the Proprietor, HENRY M. ASHTON, 63, Sankey-st., (opposite Legh-at.), Warrington.

div.head: CLIFTON.
div.p: CLIFTON.

SUPPOSED OFFENSIVE 1 RADE IN THE VILLAGE.-0a Tuesday afternoon at the fortnightly meeting of the Runcorn Rural Sanitary Authority, held at Dutton Workhouse under the presidency of Mr. J. Mclntyre. Mr. Farrington, nuisance inspector re/•,orted that in his opinion an offensive trade had been established in the townyhip of Clifton without the consent of the &mit; re Authority. He wished the matter to be referred to tee Medical Officer of Health in order that the Authority might have a report furnished thereon. The nuisareT inspector went on to say that he had visited the place referred to and had found the smell extremely offensive, so much so that he could hardly sleep that night owing to the noxieus smell which hung about his person. He had been informed that a man who worked among the material recently attended a meetinf.t. at Rock Savage and the smell was so objectionable that it almost broke up the gathering. (Laughter.) One person who had been engaged in carting the material had thrown up his employment, and he understood that one day last.week the atmosphere was so impregnated with the (inuviurn that the very horses belonging to a neighbouring farmer snorted tremendously as though they felt the effects also. (Renewed Laughter.) The stuff in its crude state fer- mented to such an extent as to burst the harrifis which contained it. Such was the case at Halton Station a few days ago, and the smell cowed the passengers and railway officials no little annoyance, The subject was finally referred to the Medical Officer of Health to report thereon. SUNDAY SCIIOOL ANNIVERSARY.—The anniversary cer- vices in connection with the Primitive Methodist Sunday school were held on Sunday. The services were numerous- ly attended, the pulpit being occupied hy the Rev. H. R..Didcock, whose remarks were listened to with close attention, The singing of the children and choir was excellent, and credit is due to Miss Clara Shore for devoting so much of her time and attention upon the children to tit them for the occasion. The collections amounted to £2, which is nearly a sovereign more than last year.

THE EXAMINER, • SATURDAY JULY 14, 1894.
WA RRINGTON COUNTY COURT.
THURSDAY.—Before His Honour Judge Wynne FfoulkeF.

CLAIM FOR TIIHES.-Mr. Hatton- (MeS"sre. R. Davies and (Jo.) claimed on behalf of the Rev. James Carson, rector of Wargrave, the sum of £6 9s. for tithe due by Mr. E.W. Santrey, of Heath Farm, Croft. Mr. Browne. solicitor, appeared on behalf of the defendant, and stated that his client had been away, and did not receive the summons until Tuesday. He then had not time to instruct his solicitor,and he (Mr. Browne) was instructed to apply for an adjournment of the case. His client believed-that the tithe in question had been redeemed, and he had written to the trustee who sold him the property, but unfortunately the man was on his holi- days.—Mr. Hatton said he had reason to believe that Mr. Browne's client was not giving him a truthful state- ment, and stated that the defendant was at Newton races the previous Saturday, and he (Mr. Hatton) had not the slightest doubt that the defendant had had full notice of the action. His Honour gave the defendant leave to oppose the claim at the next sitting of the court on the condition that he paid into court the claim and costs within 43 hours.

A DomesTlc SERVANT'S CLAIM.—PIiCebO Conway, a young woman residing with her parents at Walker's-lane, Rainhill, claimed £1 6s. Bd. as wages due, from Mr. Taylor, dentist, Museum-street, Warring- ton. Mr. P. Davies represented the delendant. The complainant stated that she was engaged as cook to the defendant for one month's trial, the wages to be at the rate of £l6 per year. She let the defendant's employ when she had worked ten days. It was through Mr. Taylor that she left, as he told her she had better clear out or he would get a policeman to her. In cross-examination witness denied that she refused to wash the windows or floors. She further denied being paid 7s. o,ld. as wages, by Mrs. Taylor in the presence of the nurse on the night prev- ious to leaving. His Honour said she was putting herself in a dangerous position. On being again cross- examined as to receiving the money she denied doing so. She admitted that she did not get up until eleven o'clock on the morning of the day she let t.—Mrs. Conway, mother of the complainant, stated that on the 9th Juno she went, in company with her husband, to the defend- ant's house, to ask for the complainant's wages. He told witness that he would not give her any money, and refused to give any reason for his action.—Mr. Davies said there must be deliberate perjury on one side or the al's% The complainant was engaged for a month on trial by Mrs. Taylor as a general servant, and her wages were to be £l6 per year. From the very first the complainant did not give satisfaction. She refused to do the work she was told to do, and on being spoken to about it,slie told the defendants to pay her the wages due.and she would go. Mrs. Taior thereupon did so in the presence of the nurse. The next morning she stayed in bed until eleven o'clock, and then went home.—Mrs. Taylor. Miss A. Leach. and Mr. Taylor all gave evidence for the defence corroborating Mr. Davies' statement. The two former stated that the com- plainant was paid her wages. Mr. Taylor said that he told the complainant's mother that the girl had received her wages. His Honour gave judgment for the defendant.

div.head: -4,...._ OUR LOCAL CHURCHES-WARRINGTON.
div.p: -4,...._ OUR LOCAL CHURCHES-WARRINGTON.
LATCEIFORD BAPTIST CHAPEL.

Sermons were preached at the above chapel on Sunday, by Dr. Parker, the president of the Brighton Grove Baptist College, Manchester. In the afternoon, the doc- tor chose his text from the Ist chapter of Revelations, 16th and 17th verses, and preached an excellent sermon to a good congregation. The evening service was a purely evangelistic one, being much appreciated by a congrc4ation whi ch filled the chapel to its utmost capacity. Two ant hems were given by the choir in a pleasing manner. The total of the two collections was the respectable sum of £lB. WYCLIFFE P.S.A. SOCIETY.

The effect of the exceptionally fine weather and boli• day season was again observable in the attendance at the above-named Society on Sunday. Mr. J. Porritt, presided. The Rev. G. Clarke, of Chester, was the speaker for the afternoon. He said he was glad that he could address those present as brothers, he being a mem- ber of the P.S.A. brotherhood. There were two institu- tions which he believed, with the help of God's Holy spirit, would play a very important part in the religious life of the future. These were the P.S.A. movement, and the Y.P.S.C.E. Societies. The object of the former was to win back lapsed Sunday school scholars, and the latter to retain young people in their schools and churchfs. The rev. gentleman then delivered an excellent addrcss on " What is religion." Miss F. Booth and Mr. Watts contributed solos. Messrs. T. Wallington and T. Hawthorn also took part in the meeting. MARTINSCROFT WESLEYAN CHAPEL.

The anr.nal school sermons, in connection with the Martinscrott Wesleyan Chapel, were preached on sun- day, the pulpit being occupied by the Rev. John Kir:lan, superintendent of the Warrington Circuit. Appr!)priate hymns were sung during the day and collections n‘ade in aid of the Sunday school. sr. LEWIS'S R.C. CHURCH, cRoFr.

On Sunday m.rninfr, and afternoon, the annual ser- mons on behalf of the schools were preached in St. Lewis's Rom? n Catholic Church. The morning preacher was the Rev. Fr. Blanchard, curate of Sc. Cuthbert's, Ihetton. The Rev. Fr. /leafy, of St. James's, Wigan, was announced zo preach in the afternoon, but he (lid not put in an appe,roince. The choir acquitted themselves cre,Vably, the solos bein!_; excellently sum,* bv Miss Battersby aryl Mr. Joseph Battersbv, of Culchah. The aLar-was tastefully dec-3rated for the occasion.

div.head: ORFORD CHURCH.
div.p: ORFORD CHURCH.

The annuli school sernionl wore preached in Orford Church on Sunday, the Rev. J. J. Longhorn occupying; the pulilt in the morning. Til9 evening preacher was the Rev. Morley Stevenson, principal of the Warrington Training College. The congregations were large. Dur- ing the day appropriate hymns were sung, and at the evening service a special anthem was creditably ren- dered by the chor. The offertories were in aid of tn.:" day arid Sunday schools.

div.head: F 1? ODSHAM.
div.p: F 1? ODSHAM.

ANNIVERSARY SERVICES.—On • Sunday mernin,g, after- noon, and evening, anniversary services were held in the Wesleyan Chapel. Mrs. Renton delivered an address at the morning service,and the Rev. R. Renton preached in tile afternoon and evening. Large congregations were present on all occasions,and the total offertories amounted to almost £33. PAROCIIIAL COMMITTEE MEETING.—The minutes of this committee, which was held on Saturday under the chairmanship of Mr. Alfred Thomas, J.P., were sub- mitted to the fortnightly meeting of the Sanitary Authority on Tuesday afternoon for the purpose of being cm firmed. The minutea showed that a letter hnl been read from Mr. Charles A. Linaker, who under- tolc to superintend the conversion of the several lamp- holes into maoholes in the Frodsham sewer.—Mr. H. G. Linaker had moved that so much of the resolution pissed at a previous meeting regarding stand pipes not tying allowed, be rescinded. This proposition was seconded by Mr. John Garber. Mr. Heywood moved a direct n, gatisrP and on being put to the meeting Mr. Linaker's motion was defeated by eight votes to three. —The tender of Messrs. Timmin's for additional works in connection with the Frodsham water scheme Was a !cepted.—The minutes were approved and passed by the Authority. San DROWNING CASE—Mr. • Churton, coroner, con- ducted an inquiry at the Queen's Head, Frodsham, on Monday afternoon, respecting the death of Allen Chris- topher Liffey, aged seven years, who was drowned at Saltport on the 2nd inst.—The evidence adduced went to show that the deceased was the son of Thomas Lilley, navvs on the railway at Ellesmere Port. The boy left his home with a young playmate on the 2nd inst. for the purpose of fishing in the Manchester Ship Canal. They caught two or three crabs, when Lilley suddenly espied another one. He ventured to secure it, but in the attempt fell into the Canal. His young companion raise I an alarm, but Lilley sunk before assistance could be rendered. Men had been grappling for the body daily after the occurrence but success had not attended their search. On Sat urda y morning at about three o'clock J. Antribus, watchman on the Canal at Saltport, saw the body floating on the surface of the water and landed it. Afterwards, it was conveyed to the Queen's Hcad.—The jury recorded a verdict of " Accidentally drowned."

_ _ EXCURSION TO EATON HALL. —On Wednesday morn- ing about 120 members and friends of the Hely Trinity Weiileyan Sunday School Alens' Bible Class journeyed by special train to Chester, from whence they proceeded on a visit to Eaton Hall and Eccl eston Ferry. Various amusements were indulged in and a very jolly timo was spent by the party. They returned to Frodshain from Chester by the 930 p.m. train, all having thoroughly enjoyed themselves. FRREMASONARY.— A meeting of the Cholmondeley Lodge of the Ancient Free and Accepted Masons was held on Tuesday evening in the Masonic Hall, Frodsham, Bro. H. W. Abernethy presiding. The attendance, which was large included Messrs. S. Davies, SW.; H. E. Heywood, J. W. ; J. Asht-n, P.M.; .1. W. Wright, secretary ; W. H. Crouchley, S.D.; J. J. VV. Pot!er J.D.; F. A. Smith, 1.G.; Dr. J. Raschen, S.S.; R. Newhouse, P.G S.; and J. Reynolds. Tyler.—Among the items of business transacted was that of passing Bro. Dr. T. J. Selby and Bro. J.G. Kydd, to the second degree —On the motion of Bro. Colonel J. Ashton, seconded by Bro. Heywood. a vote of condolence was passed to the widow f the late Bro. James Reynolds, J.P., of Fox Hill.—At the conclusion of the proceedings the bret,iren partook of an excellent supper provided by Miss Bibby.

Charles Thomal Brown, a b.,okmaker, of Plymouth. Wati indicted at the Plymouth Quarter Sessions, on Saturday, for keeping a betting house. The recorder, who doubted whether h.) could send the defendant to prison, fined him £4OO and costs.

div.head: RACE WEEK AT EARLESTOWN.
div.p: RACE WEEK AT EARLESTOWN.

The opening day of the annual race meeting at Newton Common, was favoured with fair weather, and in consequence there was a large influx of patrons of the sport. A fairly good number of piN.)ple left the town on pleasure bent, principally employes of the h. and N. tir. ity. Co., who enjoy the privilege of reaching places of popular resort at very cheap rate.,. Towards evening a heavy thunder- storm burst over the district, which had the effect of putting a damper upon the prospects of a fine cup day. The day howQver, opened fine, and as there was a prom- ise of some excellent sport, the number of visitors was said to be much in excess of previous years. The crowd on both days was generally speaking, very orderly, and with the exception of a few minor cases of gambling,the police Lad no reason to complain of the conduct of the large gathering of the people. Locally, the tradespeople closed their places wf business during Friday afternoon, re-opening at six o'clock, but on Saturday they remained open the whole of the day. Some yeys ago it was the custom to hold all the Sunday school treats on Friday, and on Saturday the senior scholars,teachers,and others had picnics to various places. The treats are now held on Whit-Monday, and there is of course no necessity to celebrate them on rate Friday. The exception to this is the

div.head: NEWTON CONGREGATIONAL SCHOOL
div.p: NEWTON CONGREGATIONAL SCHOOL

which held its annual scholars treat on Friday. Mus- tering at the school about two o'clock, the scholars num- bering about 200 were formed in procession, and headed by the Havdock brass band, with the hey. James Allatt, Mr. -Jones (supQrintendent), and Mr. Battersby, following, they proceeded through Newton village as far as the church, and returning by way of Willow-road and Mercer-street. to a field off Ashton-lane, kindly lent by Mr. W. Longton. About four o'clock buns and milk were distributed. A thunderstorm shortly after broke, which had the effect of driving the scholars to the school- r)om, several of them going home. Others returned to the field, where they remained until dusk. .During the afternoon, racing for prizes, and other.games were in- dulged in. On Saturday morning the elder scholars and teachers numbering about 50, left Earlestown by the 8.45 train for Frodsham. The day was spent in rambling about the hills and visiting the cave and ether points of in- terest. Tea was served at Mersey View and heartily enjoyed. Ciarnes and dancing were indulged in, and after a pleasing day the party reached home about 10.30, Mr. R. Owen had charge of the arrangements.

EARLESTOWN WESLEYANS. On aturday morning the select class and teachers of the Wesleyan Sunday School, numbering about 30 left Earlestown about 11.30 for Frodsham. The weather was fine during the greater part of the day and the out- ing was in consequense much enjoyed. The day was spent in rambles, games, &c., and tea, was partaken of at Mersey View. The return journey was completed abut 10.30 p.m.

div.head: EARLESTOWN BAPTISTS.
div.p: EARLESTOWN BAPTISTS.

The choir of—tii-e-1374-P-t-i;t Church and several friends, numbering about 2'.; left Eirlestown about six o'clock for Blackpool. The imrning was spent in visiting the vari- ous places of interest, and in ascending the Blackpool Tower. In the afternoon the Winter Gardens were visited, and the remainder of the day was passed on the sands. Dinner and tea were partaken of at Holden's vstiurant, and alter a very enjlyable day, Earlestown' was reached at 11.30. Mr. E. Eckersley had charge of the arrangements.

div.head: AFTER THE RACES AT NEWTON.
div.p: AFTER THE RACES AT NEWTON.

At the conclusion of the races the police had the usual gang of swindlers arraigned before the magis- trates to answer for their sins, and pay accordingly. The following composed Friday's batch, and they were tried before Mr. T. J. Gillespie, and Mr. T. H. Pearson, at the Earlestown police office. The first on the list was John Smoothly, who P.C. Foxcroft discovered smoothly swindling the gullible British public with a game called red and white horses, and hauled him and his paraphernalia to the lockup. He pleaded guilty and was ordered to pay 203. and costs for his bit of fun.—P.C. Foxcroft was also responsible for bringing to justice, Alfred Ross, and putting an end to his game of box and numbers. This also involved another fine of 203. and costs.—George Evans for playing "under and over "with a box and dice,had to pay 20s.and costs,P.C. Duncan had the merit of securing this conviction. 'The same officer secured Charles Johnson for the same offence who had to contribute a like sum to the rates.—The three card trick was represented by Frederick Connolly and who with his stock in trade was secured by P.C. Thackeray and fined 20s. and costs. He had only 2s. in his possession.—'Thomas Hildred for playing with red and white horses, had to pay 30A, and costs, the Chair- man observing that this was a worse case than the other as in consequence of the board, having a secret spring, enabling the proprietor to stop the finger wheecrever he wished, it was a direct swindle. Pricking the garter, had a representative in John McGrath, who smiled contemptuously while officer Pope was trying to explain to the magistrates how the trick was done, lie was however fined 20s. and costs.

div.head: ON SATURDAY.
div.p: ON SATURDAY.

Colonel Wood and Mr. M. McCorquodale ad- judicated on the cases brought betore them. The first was one of " Welshing," which fell to the credit of P.C. Foxcroft. The delinquents were Mark Davidson and John iall, and they were char2ed with feloniously stealing and carrying away from Newton racecourse the sum of 153.,the property of George James. The latter who hailed from Liverpool, said he was on the grand stand at the races, and saw Hall and another man making a book. He put 103. on " The Rush," which won. We went for his money, but saw no one about. He was sure of the man Hall, but could not swear to the other defendant.—P.C. Foxcroft said he was on the grand stand and saw the two defend- ants making a book, and as soon as the race was over they both left the paddock. He followed them and stopped them, when they offered t) go back and pa: the tets, bin he refused to allow therm—P.C. Duncan said he was with the other officer, and corroborated his statement. In the course of the afternoon he saw the two defendants slip out of the ground and change their coats and come back.—Davidson said he had been mak- ing a book all day and had paid all his bets. He never made any bets on the race in question. Hall said he had been clerking for the other man,and had made no bets. —They were each fined 30s. and costs.—The victim James said he would like to have his money if possible, but the magistrates said they had no power to make any order to that effect. The other cases were of the usual character, and were as under :—James Burnall, for playing "red and white horses " ; John Morrison, "box and numbers " ; Johni Coyle," under and over " ; Joseph Spooner and George Davies, "box and numbers," were all fined 20s. and costs each, the three latter going to gaol for 14 days.— James Cohen pleaded guilty to being drunk and dis- c'rderly on Thursday, and was tined 23. 6d. and costs.
THE MAYOR AND CORPORATION OF
WARRINGTON AT CHURCH.

In accordance with an announcement made at the close of the last Town Council meeting, the Mayor (Alderman Edward Greenall) and several members and officials of the Corporation, police force and tire brigade, on Sunday attended the morning service at the Parish Church. On this occasion the members of the fire brigade wore their new brass helmets for the first time, and made a very good appearance. A start was made from the Town Hall at 10 o'clock, the order of the procession being as follows : —l'olice, under the direction of the Chief Constable (Mr. Hunt) ; fire brigade, under the core'luctorship of the superintendent (Mr. Frank Turner) ; then came the Mayor, who had the Deputy Mayor (Alderman Fran- comb) on his right and the Town Clerk (Mr. J. Lyon Whittle), on his left, Alderman Wright, Councillors Muir, Hill, Baird, R. T. Fairclough, James Fairclough, Bennett and Shaw, (Alderman Harrison following behind in carriage). There were also in the procession Mr. G. F. F. White (deputy magistrates' clerk), Mr. F. Taylor (cashier at the Gas Works), Mr. Madeley (curator and librarian), and Messrs. William Pierpoint, William LawleYs, Alfred Jolley, Harry Toft, John Chidlaw, Shirlaw, and Inspector McAteer (N.S.P.C.C.). After church the procession was joined by Councillor Beaman, Mr. Longdin (borough surveyor), Mr. E. Aukland, and the following officers of the Parish Church : Messrs. John Walton' Arthur Browne, Samuel Davies, William Gill (Winmarleigh-street), Thomas Mason and T. Moores. The Borough Brass Band preceded the procession to the church and played some admirable selections, of music. There was A fair congregation at the church. After prayers were read the Rector (Rev. F. W. Willis) announced that the new Parish Church Day School, called "Fairfield Schools," would be opened on the fol- lowing Thursday be the Hon. John Powys,• son of the Right Hon. Lord Lilford, at four p.m. The buildings had cost £6,C00, and a sum of £2,000 was still required before they could be declared free from debt. The Rev. G. B. Thurston, M.A., was the preacher and he chose for his text the words, 'And King David said to Orman, Nay but I will verily buy it for the full price, for I will net take that which is thine for the Lord, nor offer burnt offerings wi!l.eiit cost." In concluding an excellent address the r :•entleman thanked the Mayor and Cor- poration fol• t ikir presence there that morning.

div.p: jABEZ BALFOUR.
DECISION AGAINST' EXTRADITION.
Bunxos --AYRES, THußsDny.—The Federal judge declares ti,at the Extradition Treaty between Great Britain anti Ar.gentirm is not applicable to the ease of Jabcz Balfour.

div.head: DRUNK AND INCAPABLE.
div.p: DRUNK AND INCAPABLE.

At the Tow—n-iia-1-1, Newton, on -Wednesday morn- ing, before Mr. T. J. Gillespie, Catherine Fitzgerald was charged with being drunk in Iligh-st.,Newton, on Monday evening. The officer stated that she was SO drunk that she could not walk, and he 'aad 10 convey her to the Police Station in a wheelbalrow. She was fined '2,?. Gd. and costs.
