div.head: SUICIDE OF A SOLDIER AT ORFOR.D BARRACKS.
div.p: SUICIDE OF A SOLDIER AT ORFOR.D BARRACKS.
A PATHETIC LETTER.

At twelve o'clock on Tuesday morning Colour- Sergeant James Walsh, of B. Company, 3rd Batta- lion Liverpool Regiment, committed suicide at his quarters in Orford Barracks. The deceased was 33 years of age, and had been in the service a number of years. He was president of the sergeants' mess,and was very much respected by all who knew him. The body was taken to the hospital to await the inquest which took place on Thursday in the Parade Room, at the Police Station before Mr. trighouse, county coroner. Mary Walsh, was the first witness called, and she said the deceased was her husband, and a colour-sergeant in the regiment stationed at Orford Barracks. She last saw him alive at half-past eleven on Tuesday morning, in his quarters at Orford Barracks. The deceased had been low-spirited and depressed for some time, in con- sequence of his health being bad. His eyes were bad, and he could not see to make up his books. She said that deceased had also received an injury to his head about three years ago, caused by a pole falling upon him.

Catherine Creagan, mother-in-law of the deceased, and residing in Marsh-st., stated that the deceased had been depressed and could not see properly. The last time she saw him alive was on Tuesday, at her daugh- ter's house in the Barracks. Shortly before she left, the deceased went into another room to try and balance his books, and about ten minutes after she heard a report, but did not think much of it until her daughter (the wife of the deceased) asked her to go and see what it was, thinking it might be one of the children. She got up and opened the door and saw the deceased stretched out on the sofa with the gun lying across his body. On examination it was found that the deceased had taken his shoes and stockings off and tied one of his toes to the trigger of the gun, and so fired it off, blowing his brains out.

Colour-Sergeant Alfred Savage said that he knew the deceased intimately. He had last seen him alive at the sergeant's mess on Tuesday morning. For some time past he had noticed that the deceased was strange in his manner, but had no suspicion that he contemplated suicide.

Here the Coroner produced a letter, and asked Savage if the writing on it was that of the dead man. He re- plied that it was. The letter, which appeared to have been written some time before the deceased's death, contained the following "Dear Mary,—Bring up the two—David and James —not in the wa.y of their father. It is my only wish for them to look to their work and keep away from the drink. My head is almost bursting! lam too full to see you ! I can only say I am to.) much behind in my work. I am also ashamed to see my officer. Every- thing connected with the accounts making up the ser- geants' mess account,is in the blue book. God bless you! —Your Jimmy. On no account must Mr. Ash, the captain Of my company,be put to any expense. Brooks has lost his kit."

Lieutenant Clarke was the last witness called, and he stated that the deceased's work was to take charge of the Company's accounts. He had noticed the deceased's strangeness of manner. The jury returned a verdict of "Suicide whilst temporarily insane."
SUDDEN DEATH IN THE MARKET.

On Saturday morning, Mary Massey, wife of Samuel Massey, market gardener, Walton Inferior, died very suddenly in the yard of John Stocks, hairdresser, in the Market Place, at 7-15. The deceased woman got up very early and prepared her produce to bring t 9 the Warrington Market. She had her breakfast at 5-30 a.m., and shortly after- wards complained of pains in her chest. ihe took something to ease the pain, and then left home for Warrington where she arrived at 6-35. The pains in her chest continued to trouble her and she there- fore went to sit down in Mr. Stock's yard. She had not been in the yard long, when Mr. Stocks noticed her fall. A man named Frank Birch went to her assistance, but she died before medical aid could be procured. Mrs. Massey had attended the Warrington Market for years, and had never com- plained of illness except a slight touch of spasms occasionally. The coroner was notified of the death, but he did not consider an inquest necessary.
IMPERIAL PARLIAMENT.
THURSDAY.

In the House of Commons on Thursday evening, Mr. H. GARDNER informed Mr. CHAPLIN that there did not seem to be any prospect at present of dispensing with the statutory requirements for slaughtering Canadian cattle at the port of entry. Mr. H. GLADSTONE in answer to a question said the reason why there was no statute of Cromwell within the precincts of the House was that the Committee which dealt with this subject were not unanimous in regard to Cromwell's claims. There were no funds available for a statue, but he should be very glad to consider the matter.

Sir W. HARCOURT, at the instance of Mr. BARTLEY, had to explain why a Civil List pension had been conferred on Professor Rhys-Davids, an eminent Oriental scholar ; but Mr. BARTLEY was not satisfied, and made a refer- ence to the Professor's connection with the National Liberal Club which drew forth shouts of "Oh !" The Rouse resumed consideration of the Budget Bill as amended in Committee.

The House of Lords, on the motion of the Earl of CIIkSTERFIELD (Treasurer of the Household), read a second time the Coalmines (Check Weighers) Bill, a measure designed to prevent improper influence in the appointment of check weightnen, and to leave colliers absolutely free in the choice of this officer.

div.head: COAL TRADE.
div.p: THE COAL TRADE.
THE NEWCASTLE CONFERENCE.

A Conference of miners representing all the colliery districts in the United Kingdom was held on Thursday at Newcastle-on-Tyne. The Conference was summoned mainly for two purposes—to discuss the condition of the Scotch coal strike, and to endeavour to agree upon a national policy for the protection of miners' labour. Delegates were present representing 391,000 men. Northumberland, which has now decided to throw in its lot with the Federation, was represented ; and although no delegate was present on Thursday frNin Durham, that county will be represented at the subse- quent conference on the question of a national policy. On the question of the Scotch strike Mr. Smillie presented a report as to the present condition of affairs, and it was unanimously decided to render what finan- cial aid was possible to the strikers; and miners out- side the Federation were also recommended to pay. a levy of one shilling a week along with the members of the Federation. There was consider- able discussion as to whether the money should be distributed among union and non-union men alike, but ultimately it was resolved that it should be divided according to membership of the Federation in each of the districts of Scotland, allowing the local com- mittees to deal with it as they might think proper. It was stated thot £15,000 was handed to the Scotch miners as the result of levies made on the Federation. The debate on the subject of a national policy was opened, and adjourned until to-day.

div.head: NOTES BY THE WAY AT EARLESTOWN.
div.p: NOTES BY THE WAY AT EARLESTOWN.
BY AN OCCASIONAL CORRESPONDENT.

The great annual holiday so far as Earlestown ,is concerned, commonly known as Newton Races, is now a thing of the past, and excluding the refresh- ment house keepers, I do not know that anybody locally is any the better for it. Even the caterers for the inner man did not get off unscathed, for I hear that one of them was unfortunate enough to have to supply about half-a-dozen visitors with a dinner gratuitously. Of course it will be under- stood be did not do this with a free will, but by force of circumstances was forced to the inevitable. Now if I kept a restaurant, I should make it a rule to receive payment for the dinners I supplied, immediately I put them on the table, especially when I had chance customers to deal with such as these, and then the diners, could please themselves whether they ate the dinner or not. Perhaps the victim will profit by the experience gained.

---, As usual there was a great crowd of visitors to the town, but on the whole they behaved them- selves remarkably well, and the police had very little cause to complain. There was the customary hangers on to such gatherings, who gat their living by means not particularly square. Several of these fell into the hands of the police, and had to suffer in proportion to their misdeeds. It is surprising what tricks men will resort to in order to empty the pockets of their fellow men. Everybody knows the game of chance called" red and white horses" how that on a board representing a table is a circle on which is painted horses of the colours named, in the centre being an iron finger working on a pivot. The game is fair enough if fairly played, and everyone has an equal chance, bu.; it is not everybody who knows that beneath the table is a secret spring worked by the operator, and by which he can win or lose as he choses. Such is the case however,and, as the magistrate said, it is a direct swindle.

Catherine Fitzgerald had a ride the other day at Newton, which for the time being would no doubt be thought cheap, but which in the end Catherine would think was considerably dearer than walk- ing. Her conveyance was a one wheel chaise, and of course when people -choose such luxurious means of locomotion, they must expect to pay for the privilege. Catherine was drunk, very drunk, and as her legs refused to carry her, she had to be con- veyed to her destination in the manner described, by an official in uniform. For this little bit of luxury she had to pay 28. 6d. and the costs of appearing before a magistrate. Think of this ye that imbibe too freely of the essence of barleycorn, and when you desire to enter the precincts of a police station, do not have to requisition a one wheel chaise.

The County authorities are evidently much more thoughtful of the comfort of their police officers, than those who rule the ',Boroughs. A policeman is only a human being after all, and it is natural that he should feel the heat of a summers day, like any other ordinary mortal. Week in and week out, winter and summer he is compelled to wear the same thick tight-fitting tunic, and I do not doubt that at times he finds it very uncomfortable. The authorities however have taken compassion upon the policemen, and have served out to them, light and loose fitting tunics, which can be worn without the regulation belt. I cannot say that the tunic is a very handsome affair,but that is only a secondary matter. The principal factor being its lightness and comfort, and I feel sure the officers will appreciate the intention. To complete the outfit they want white helmets to be worn when the sun is glaring down in all its intensity.

It is an ill wind that blows nobody good, at least that is what the various ministers embraced in the Winwick Rectory Act. It appears from the answer to a question asked by our hon. member in the 1-louse of Commons that sufficient funds have been raised from the sale of the estate to warrant the Commissioners making, what I suppose is a preiiin- inary division, the amount running to something like £450 per year. This means that the various rectors, and vicars in Newton, Golborne, Lowton, Croft, and Earlestown, will have their stipends raised to £3OO per year. Some of them are receiv- ing very handsome advances, and I only wish I was one of the number.

div.head: STOCKrON HEATH.
div.p: STOCKrON HEATH.

ST. THOMAS' CHURCH INSTITUTE.—The members of the above institute, accompanied by their friends and the Rev. H. R. C. Vernon, had a very enjoyable pic-nic to Froclshani on Saturday, Though the weather at the time of startin, was inclined to be wet it cleared off on the arrival at Frodsham and remained fine the remainder of the time. The committee who had the matter in hand had made excellent arrangements and are to be congratulated ion the success which attended their labours.

PAnocutaL COMMITTEL—On Tuesday afternoon the minutes of the meeting of this Committee, held on tho 6th inst., were snbmitted to the fortnightly meeting of the Runcorn Rural Sanitary Authority, at Dutton Work- house, Mr. John Mclntyre occupying the chair. The minutes showed that it was decided on the motion of Mr. Westbrook, seconded by Mr. Thomas Hall, that the Clerk write to the Warrington Corporation, calling atten- tion to the unsuflicient supply of water to the higher parts of Stockton Heath and Birch Dale, and asking that this be immediately remedied. It was resolved that Messrs. Hall, Longland, and Westbrook be appointed a deputation to wait upon the Waterworks Committee with reference to the subject. Mr. Silcock explained that Messrs. Prescot and Jones had made good the road referred to by Mr. Leader Williams to the satisfactiono f the Manchester Ship Canal Company, and certified that they were entitled to a further payment of £ll in res- pect thereof. It was decided on the motion of Mr. Dawn. port, seconded by Mr. Shackleton, that the firm be paid the amount named. Tenders for the erection of the sewerage works along Chester-road were received and opened. They numbered eight,and it was resolved that the one forwarded by Messrs. Sayer and Randle, for £169 103. 61 be accepted, and that application be made to the Local Government Board for their sanction to a loan of £2OO, for the construction of the works.—The minutes were confirmed by the authority.

COUNTY COUNCILS OF LANCASHIRE AND ST. HELENS. (PRES COT UNION.) ARDER of Joint Committee dealing with Poor Law Union In two Counties, and providing for (1) division of Town- ships into Wards for Eleetion of Guardians and Rural District Couneillors, (2) fixing number of Guardians and Rural Dis- trict Councillors for each Township. Ward, &c., and (3) pro- viding for Simultaneous Retirement of Guardians and Rural District Councillors. • THE Local, GOVERNMENT Ater, 1894." TO THE COUNTY COUNCIL OF THE COUNTY PALATINE OF LANCASTER; TO THE COUNTY COUNCIL OF THE COUNTY BOROUGH OF ST. HELENS; To the Guardians of the Poor of the Prescot Poor Law Union, in the County of Lancaster; To the Overseers of the Townships mentionedln the Schedule to this Order ; To all others whom it may concern. W EREAS by Section 60 of' The Local Government Act, 1894," it is provided that the Courcil of each County may from time to time by Order fix the number of Guardians or Rural District Councillors to be elected for each Parish within their County, and for these purposes may exercise power of adding Parishes to each other and dividing Parishes into Wards similar to those which by the Acts relating to the If. lief of the Poet' are for the purpose of the election of Guardians vested in the Local Government Board, and that where a Poor Law Union is situate in more than one County the power under the said Section of fixing or altering the number of Guardians or Rural District Councillors shall be exercised by a Joint Committee of the Councils of the Counties concerned; And whereas by an Order of the Local Government Board, dated the 25th day of October, 1832, it is provided that the whole of the Guardians of the Prescot Union shall retire to- gether at the end of every third year, and no application has been made to alter or vary such Order; And whereas it is provided by Section 24 Sub-Section 4of the same Act that the provisions of that Act, with respect to the election and term of office and retirement of Guardians, shall apply to Rural District Councillors; And whereas the Poor Law Union of Prescot is situate partly within the Administrative County of Lancaster and partly within the County Borough of Bt. Helens ; And whereas in the County e alatine of Lancaster the area for rating purposes has from time immemorial been described by the term Township, and it is desirable that the ancient name should be retained in this Order; And whereas a Joint Committee has been appointed by the Councils of the said Counties to act under the Sections here- inbefore recited ; And whereas the said Joint Committee have taken into consideration the ease of the said Prescot Union, and have in accordance with Section 57 of " The Local Government Act, 1888," and the Orders of the Local Government Board in that behalf caused inquiries to be made and notices to be given as prescribed by the said Act and Orders : Now therefore we, the said Joint Committee, in pursuance of the powers given by "The Local Government Acts, 1888 and 1894," do hereby order as follows :- 1. Each of the Townships mentioned in the first column of the first Schedule hereunder written shall, for the pur- poses of the election of Guardians, be divided into the Wards of which the names are stated in the second column of the said Schedule, and the boundaries of such Ward In the third column of the said Schedule. 2.—The number of G-uard:ans to be elected for each of the Townships or Wards mentioned in the first column of the second Schedule hereunder written shall be the number stated cpposite to the name of that Township or Ward in the second column of the said Schedule, and the number of District Councillors to be elected for each of the Town- ships shall be the number stated opposite to the name of that Township in the third column eat the said Schedule. 3.—The Guardians and Rural District Councillors to be elected in pursuance of this Order shall retire together on the 15th day of April, 1893, and in every third year there- after until it is otherwise di reetcd in pursuance of the said Act. 4. This Order shall come into operation upon the appointed day as defined by Section 84 of " The Local Government Act, 1894." SCHEDULE I.
1 Name of Township, Ward, or Group.

IMPERIAL PARLIAMENT. ' MONDAY. In the Flouse of Commons on Monday evening Sir W. Heacounr,replying to Mr.T.W.LEoH,said he was not in a position to state until the Budget was disposed of what facilities the Government would be able to give to the Miners' Eight Hours Bill or any other measure. The House considered the Budget Bill as amended in Committee. Mr. CHAPLIN moved a clause enabling an owner of agricultural land unable to pay the estate duty except by a forced sale to require the authorities to accept so much of his land as would be equivalent to the duty. Sir W. HARCOURT said the idea was absurd. The clause was rejected by 185 to 147. Other amend- ments were defeated by majorities ranging from thirty to fifty-seven. Shortly after midnight Mr. BRYCE moved that the Railway and Canal Traffic Bill be referred to the Stand- ing Committee on Trade. Opposition was raised from the Conservative benches, and the motion had to be adjourned. In the House of Lords the Lord Chancellor informed Lord Stanley of Alderlev that he could not interfere in the question of licensing in the island of Lewis,where,as reported, the renewal of certain licences had been re- fused, although there were only three public-houses on the island, while the pepulation was 33,000. The In- dustrial Schools Act (1886) Amendment Bill and the Quarries (Inspection) Bill were read a second time. TUESDAY. In the House of Commons on Tuesday evening Sir E. GREY informed Sir E. A. BARTLETT that in the event of the English occupation of Port Hamilton ceasing, Russia undertook not to take Curean territory under any circumstances. Mr. A. MORLEY, in answer to Mr. SCHWANN, said he could not accede to the application of the Manchester male telegraph staff for abolition of classification and improved rates of pay. The application was refused by his predecessor, and he saw 114 i grounds for departing from that decision. Consideration of the Finance Bill as amended in Com- mittee was resumed. Mr. BurcuEn moved to exempt gilts to the nation or to municipal or other public bodies. Sir W. HARCOURT said he was willing to give the Trea- sury discretion to remit duty in reference to gifts to the nation or to any county or town council. Mr. BALFOUR suggested that universities should be included in the- benefit. Sir War. HARCOURT said he was not at all indis- posed to consider this suggestion, but there must be some definite limitation. The amendment was then with- drawn. The Parochial Electors (Registration Acceleration) Bill was read a third time at midnight.

DEATH OF SIR GILBERT GREENALL, BART. - Sir Gilbert Greenall, Bart., died on Tuesday after- noon, at about 3.30, at Tilstone, near Tarporley, the residence of his son, at the ripe old age of SS. fhe news was not unexpected, for Sir Gilbert had been gradually sinking for some weeks past. The sad event was speedily known in Warrington, and flags were hoisted half mast high, as a mark of respect to the late baronet, on the Town Hall, and the Liberal and Conservative Clubs. A SKETCH OF HIS CAREER. Sir Gilbert comes of an old country family and was born May 11, '-.'1.806, being the youngest son of the late Mr. Edward Greenall, of Wilderspool. His grandfather was Mr. Thomas Greenall, of St. Helens, who at about the middle Of the eighteenth century founded the brewery, in connection with which,Sir Gilbert was so well-known. Sir Gilbert was not the only member of parliament, in his family, for he had an elder brother, Mr. Peter Green- ; all, who represented Wigan in 1841, and who died at St. Helens in 1845, and was interred in St. Mary's Church. . Sir Gilbert when a boy attended a private school in War- rington, and subsequently went along with his twin . brother (Archdeacon Greenall) to Dr. Pulford's school in Liverpool. His business career commenced when he was seventeen years of age, when he left school, and returned to Wilderspool. He has been connected with the brewery from that time to the time of his death, being the largest shareholder, and head of the firm. He was married in March, 1836, to Miss Mary Claue,hton, daughter of the late Mr. David Claughton of Haydock. He had no child- ren by this marriage. In 1864, Sir Gilbert, then Mr. Greenall, married again,his second wife being Susannah daughter of the late Mr. John Louis Knapp, by whom he had three children,a son and two daughters—Mr.Gilbert and Miss Susannah and Miss Bertha Greenall. Mr. Gilbert Greene'', who succeeds to the title was born on March , 30, 1867, and attained his majority on Good Friday. 1888, on which occasion, there were great festivities. Sir Gilbert was the oldest magistrate in the county of Lan- cashire being created J.P. for the West Derby hundred on January 12, 1843. He was also a magistrate for Cheshire. He has also been High Sheriff for Cheshire, and Deputy Lieutenant for Lancashire. He sat in Par- liament almost continually from 1847 to 1892, there only having been two intervals in which he went into an enforced retirement, viz., in the Parliaments of 1868- 74 and 1880-85. He was first chosea as the CONSERVATIVE CANDIDATE for Warrington in 1847, on the occasion of the retirement from public life of the late Mr. Ireland Black- burn who had represented Warrington from 1835 to 1847. At that time, the number of electors in Warrington was very small, and he defeated the Liberal candidate, Mr. W. Alleard by 29 votes. In the succeeding elections up to 1868, he was-elected unopposed, and his services appear to have been much appreciated at that time, for in 1864, during the mayoralty of Alderman Holmes. a compli- mentary public dinner was given to him in the Public Hall "in acknowledgment of his services as representa- tive of this borough in Parliament during the past six- teen years." Colanel Wilson Patten, M.P. (afterwards Lord Winmarleigh) was the chairman, and tickets were 15s. each, so that the affair was a very select one. Pre- vious to this time, he had laid the foundation of the Public Hall in Rylands-st., which has since been acquired by the Royal Court Theatre proprietors. In 1868, when the suffrage had been greatly extended, the Liberals of the town determined ta make a strong effort to capture the seat which had been consistently Tory since 1831. They accordingly chose as their candidate the late Mr. Peter Rylands, and a fierce contest was fought,. This election was also memorable as being the last one in Warrington, ever fought by open voting. The scene at the hustings was a very memorable one,t he excitement being intense, and at one time, it was feared that a free fight between the two parties would have resulted. This misfortune was averted, however. On the election day, every exertion was put forward by ' each side to bring up their supporters to give in their votes. The result was an unexpected victory for Mr. Rylands who obtained a majority of 27 votes. This result was a great blow to the Conservatives of Warrington. and they endeavoured by means of a petition to have the election declared void. It appears that a number of Conserva- tives who were more or less exhilarated, instead of giv- ing their voting tickets to the polling clerk, had given them to the Conservative agent who assured them ti al it was " all right." Baron Martin who tried the petitien however declared the election legal, and exonerated the polling clerk and the Mayor (Councillor Nield), who had been the butt of a great amount of abuse from the local Tories, from all blame. This election was a great dis- appointment to Mr. Greenall, and he was determined on the first opportunity to turn the tables upon his opp, n- eut. He had six years to wait however, and in 1874, the same two gentlemen again core ested the seat. The result was the RETURN OF MR. GREENALL, the figures being Greenall, 2,381 ; Hy!, nes. 2,2ol,majority for Mr. Greenall 180. His gratifica ion at this result was well expressed in his address of ti anas to the electors. It ran as follows :—" Gentlemen I cannot sufficiently thank you for the unprecedented exertions you have made on my behalf, and for the triumphant victory you have achieved. This day compensates for the disap- pointments of the past, and henceforth I shall speak of them no more; we are again one community, and I have no other politic al object than the good of our cern- inon country, and of the town with which I have been so long connected. Once more I feel that I represent you all, the differences of party are obliterated, and that if differences of opinion remain,hostility of feeling exists no more.—! am, &c., GILBERT GREENALL." It was during the existence of the Parliament of 1874 80, that Mr. Greenall received his baronetcy. The honour was c inferred upon him on March 22, 1876, and the occasion was fittingly celebrated in Warrington by an aedress from the Corporation, a dinner at the Town Hall, a pre- sentation from his constituents, arid a series of congra- tulatory ward meetings. In 1880 Sir Gilbert had again to face a contested election, his opponent this time be- ing the late Mr. John Gordon McMinnies, Mr. Peter 11$ - lairds in the meantime being returned to Parliamr nt ar Liberal member for Burnley. This election was again a very keen one, and the result was a complete OVERTHROW OF THE TORY PARTY, the fioures being McMinnies 3,002, Greenall 2,473, a Liberal majority of 529. A rather amusiee fiasco took place at the declaration of the pod on this occasion. The Mayor (Alderman J. It. Pickmere) had adopted the unusual method of reading the names of the candidates in their alphabetical order, and of course Sir Gilbert Greenall's name was called out first. The Tories thinking that they had won the election, received the announcement with a great out- burst of cheering, and the spirits of the Liberals were correspondingly cast down. When;however, the figure s were given out, the Liberals were in a state of great jubilation. In the meantime, Sir Gilbert was awaiting the result at the Lion Hotel along with Mr. Whitley, M.P. for Liverpool, who was prepared with a speech of congratulation on the occasien of another Tory victory in Warrington. Toe false news of the election of Sir Gilbert had arrived at the " Lion." and the baronet was warmly congratulated on his " election " for the good old borough. Enthusiastic Tories surrounded him, as- suriee hire that he had defeated Mr. McMinnies by 32 votes ! flow such intelligence arrived it is hard to tell, t'ut Sir Gilbert was very chary at accepting the state- ment, and said he would wait till his agent arrived. Mille the congratulations were being very profusely tendered, a young gentleman arrived with the astound- ing intelligence that Mr. McMinnies was a winner by 600 votes! The veracity of this was at once challenged, but immediately afterwards the voice of Mr. Robert Davies was heard at the bottom of the staircase shout- ing, " WCre 529 on the wrong side." Sir Gilbert at once sought the Ma of a friendly chair, and the Liver- pool champion subsided into a corner, sinking on a sofa with an exclamation of astonishment. Sir Gilbert was advised not to appear at the window, though a noisy crowd was waiting below, but was advised to return home at once. Mr. Hunt, the Chief Co ristable,who was present, at once offered his all, and the defeated candi- date was conveyed to Walton Hall by a circuitous route. Thus ended the 1880 election, and Sir Glbert was in comparative retirement for the next five years. SINGULAR ABSENTMINDEDNESS. FORGOT THE NAME OF HIS BRIDE. Some remarkable instances of absence of mind in great men are to be found in collections of aria. A Dutchman seems to have surpassed anything of the kind yet per- petrated. He is a widower, and he presented himself a few dqys ago at the Registiar's in a little village near Amsterdam to give notice of his intended marriage. On being asked the name of the bride, however, he declared he could not remember it, and he had to be sent away in order that he might get the desired information. +On SAINT SWITHIN'S DAY AND THE APPLE. Though few of us believe now that if it rain on St. Swithin's Day—July 15-4 will be wet for the forty following days, still, it is com'c to watch the relief that is felt should' the Saints day be dry. There is however, one advantage to be derived from a literal fulfilling of the ancient proverb. It is sad that should the weather be wet during the forty days, it will be all the better for the apples, which, in such case, will grow large and juicy ere ripening.
